AWS IAM — Secure Access & Permissions
description: Security foundation: Users, Groups, Roles, Policies, MFA, least-privilege, and cross-account access.
subtitle: AWS IAM — Identity & Access Management
objectives: Explain the difference between IAM Users, Groups, and Roles
Write IAM policies using the Effect/Action/Resource model
Apply the principle of least privilege to production workloads
Configure MFA for root and IAM users
Implement cross-account access using AssumeRole with ExternalId
Use IAM Policy Simulator and Access Analyzer to audit permissions
Troubleshoot AccessDenied errors using CloudTrail and policy simulation

content.html:
🔐
IAM is the Gateway to Every AWS Service
Every single API call to AWS — whether from the Console, CLI, SDK, or another service — is authenticated and authorized by IAM. If you don't understand IAM, you can't secure anything in AWS. It's the single most important service to master.

The Core Problem IAM Solves

Without IAM: Everyone uses the root account with full admin access. One compromised credential → entire AWS account owned. No audit trail, no access controls, no compliance.

With IAM: Every human and service gets a unique identity with only the exact permissions they need. Every action is logged. Temporary credentials expire automatically.

IAM ComponentWhat It IsWhen to Use
UserPermanent identity with long-lived credentialsIndividual humans (minimize usage — prefer SSO)
GroupCollection of Users that share policiesOrganize users by team/role (Developers, Admins, ReadOnly)
RoleTemporary identity assumed by services or usersLambda functions, EC2 instances, cross-account access
PolicyJSON document defining Allow/Deny permissionsAttached to Users, Groups, or Roles
⚠️
Never Use the Root Account for Daily Work
The root account has unrestricted access to everything. Enable MFA on root immediately, lock it away, and create IAM Users/Roles for all operations. AWS explicitly recommends this in the Well-Architected Framework.

content.title: How Every AWS API Call is Authorized

nodes.label: API Caller
nodes.description: Any entity making an AWS API call: Console user, CLI script, Lambda function, or another AWS service.

nodes.label: SigV4 Signing
nodes.description: Every request is signed with AWS Signature Version 4 using access key + secret key (or STS temporary credentials). This proves the caller's identity cryptographically.

nodes.label: IAM Policy Engine
nodes.description: IAM evaluates ALL applicable policies: identity-based, resource-based, SCPs, session policies, permission boundaries. Default: IMPLICIT DENY. Explicit Deny always wins.

eventPayload.Rule: Explicit Deny > Explicit Allow > Implicit Deny

nodes.label: AWS Service
nodes.description: If IAM allows the request, it reaches the target service (S3, DynamoDB, Lambda, EC2, etc.) and the action is executed.

nodes.label: CloudTrail
nodes.description: Every API call (allowed or denied) is logged in CloudTrail. This provides a complete audit trail for compliance and incident investigation.

content.html:
1. IAM Policy Structure

Every IAM policy is a JSON document with this structure:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "AllowS3ReadOnly",
    "Effect": "Allow",              // Allow or Deny
    "Action": [                     // What actions
      "s3:GetObject",
      "s3:ListBucket"
    ],
    "Resource": [                   // On what resources
      "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket",
      "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"
    ],
    "Condition": {                  // Under what conditions
      "IpAddress": {
        "aws:SourceIp": "203.0.113.0/24"
      }
    }
  }]
}

2. Policy Evaluation Logic

  1. Default: Everything is IMPLICITLY DENIED
  2. IAM evaluates all applicable policies (identity + resource + SCP + boundary)
  3. If ANY policy has an Explicit Deny → DENIED (always wins)
  4. If a policy has an Explicit Allow AND no Deny → ALLOWED
  5. Otherwise → IMPLICITLY DENIED

3. Identity-Based vs Resource-Based Policies

TypeAttached ToSpecifies Principal?Cross-Account?
Identity-BasedUser, Group, or RoleNo (implied by attachment)Requires AssumeRole
Resource-BasedThe resource itself (S3 bucket, SQS queue, etc.)Yes — "Principal" field requiredAllows direct cross-account without AssumeRole

4. IAM Roles & AssumeRole

Roles provide temporary credentials via STS (Security Token Service). A role has:

  • Trust Policy: WHO can assume this role (Principal)
  • Permission Policy: WHAT the role can do once assumed

Lambda, EC2, ECS all use roles — they never have long-lived access keys.

5. Permission Boundaries

A permission boundary is a policy that sets the maximum permissions an identity can have. Even if the identity policy grants s3:*, if the boundary only allows s3:GetObject, only GetObject works. Used for delegation: "Create any role you want, but it can never access production databases."

6. MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)

  • Enable on root account immediately — non-negotiable
  • Use Condition: {"Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}} to require MFA for sensitive actions
  • Support: Virtual MFA (Authenticator apps), U2F hardware keys, hardware TOTP tokens

content.title: IAM Policy Management with Boto3

languages.label: Create Policy & Role
languages.code:
import boto3
import json
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

iam = boto3.client('iam')

def create_least_privilege_role(role_name, service_principal, policy_document):
    """
    Create an IAM Role with least-privilege permissions.
    
    Args:
        role_name: Name for the IAM role
        service_principal: AWS service that assumes this role (e.g., 'lambda.amazonaws.com')
        policy_document: Dict with the permission policy
    """
    # 1. Create the Trust Policy — WHO can assume this role
    trust_policy = {
        "Version": "2012-10-17",
        "Statement": [{
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": {
                "Service": service_principal
            },
            "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
        }]
    }

    # 2. Create the Role
    role_response = iam.create_role(
        RoleName=role_name,
        AssumeRolePolicyDocument=json.dumps(trust_policy),
        Description=f'Least-privilege role for {service_principal}',
        MaxSessionDuration=3600,  # 1 hour max session
        Tags=[
            {'Key': 'Environment', 'Value': 'production'},
            {'Key': 'ManagedBy', 'Value': 'automation'}
        ]
    )
    role_arn = role_response['Role']['Arn']
    logger.info("Created role: %s (%s)", role_name, role_arn)

    # 3. Create and attach the Permission Policy — WHAT the role can do
    policy_name = f'{role_name}-policy'
    policy_response = iam.create_policy(
        PolicyName=policy_name,
        PolicyDocument=json.dumps(policy_document),
        Description=f'Least-privilege policy for {role_name}'
    )
    policy_arn = policy_response['Policy']['Arn']

    # 4. Attach policy to role
    iam.attach_role_policy(RoleName=role_name, PolicyArn=policy_arn)
    logger.info("Attached policy %s to role %s", policy_name, role_name)

    return {'roleArn': role_arn, 'policyArn': policy_arn}


# Example: Create a Lambda execution role
lambda_policy = {
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "AllowDynamoDBCRUD",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "dynamodb:GetItem",
                "dynamodb:PutItem",
                "dynamodb:UpdateItem",
                "dynamodb:DeleteItem",
                "dynamodb:Query"
            ],
            "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:123456789012:table/Users"
        },
        {
            "Sid": "AllowCloudWatchLogs",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "logs:CreateLogGroup",
                "logs:CreateLogStream",
                "logs:PutLogEvents"
            ],
            "Resource": "arn:aws:logs:us-east-1:123456789012:*"
        }
    ]
}

# create_least_privilege_role('MyLambdaRole', 'lambda.amazonaws.com', lambda_policy)

explanations.text: Trust Policy defines WHO can assume this role. The Principal field specifies the AWS service. For cross-account, Principal would be an account ARN.
MaxSessionDuration limits how long temporary credentials from AssumeRole last (1-12 hours). Default is 1 hour. Shorter = more secure.
The permission policy follows least privilege: only specific DynamoDB actions on ONE specific table, plus CloudWatch Logs for observability. No s3:* or dynamodb:*.

languages.label: Policy Simulator
languages.code:
import boto3
import json

iam = boto3.client('iam')

def simulate_policy(role_arn, actions, resource_arns):
    """
    Simulate IAM policy evaluation — test what a role can do
    WITHOUT actually calling the service.
    
    Use this to audit permissions before deploying to production.
    """
    response = iam.simulate_principal_policy(
        PolicySourceArn=role_arn,
        ActionNames=actions,
        ResourceArns=resource_arns
    )

    results = []
    for result in response['EvaluationResults']:
        action   = result['EvalActionName']
        decision = result['EvalDecision']  # 'allowed' or 'implicitDeny' or 'explicitDeny'
        matched  = result.get('MatchedStatements', [])

        status = '✅ ALLOWED' if decision == 'allowed' else '❌ DENIED'
        results.append({
            'action': action,
            'decision': decision,
            'status': status,
            'matchedStatements': len(matched)
        })
        print(f"  {status}: {action} → {decision}")

    return results


# Test: Can this role read from S3?
simulate_policy(
    role_arn='arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/MyLambdaRole',
    actions=['s3:GetObject', 'dynamodb:PutItem', 'ec2:TerminateInstances'],
    resource_arns=['arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*']
)

# Expected output:
#   ❌ DENIED: s3:GetObject → implicitDeny
#   ✅ ALLOWED: dynamodb:PutItem → allowed
#   ❌ DENIED: ec2:TerminateInstances → implicitDeny

content.expectedOutput:
Created role: MyLambdaRole (arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/MyLambdaRole)
Attached policy MyLambdaRole-policy to role MyLambdaRole

items.title: AccessDenied — Implicit Deny
items.error: An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the PutObject operation
items.cause: No policy explicitly allows the action. IAM defaults to implicit deny. The role/user simply doesn't have the required permission.
items.fix: Identify the missing action using CloudTrail (look for errorCode: AccessDenied). Add the specific action and resource ARN to the identity or resource policy. Use IAM Policy Simulator to verify.

items.title: AccessDenied — Explicit Deny overriding Allow
items.error: CI/CD pipeline fails with AccessDenied despite having s3:PutObject in the role policy
items.cause: An S3 bucket policy or SCP contains an explicit Deny that overrides the Allow. Explicit Deny ALWAYS wins in IAM evaluation.
items.fix: Check ALL policies: identity policy, resource policy (S3 bucket policy), SCP (Organizations), and permission boundary. An explicit Deny in ANY of these blocks the action.

items.title: AssumeRole fails cross-account
items.error: AssumeRoleUnauthorizedAccess when assuming a role in another account
items.cause: The target role's trust policy doesn't include the source account ARN, or ExternalId is missing/wrong.
items.fix: Update the trust policy Principal to include the source account/role ARN. Add Condition with sts:ExternalId if required. Verify the source has sts:AssumeRole permission for the target role ARN.

items.title: New IAM user can't log into Console
items.error: User created but cannot sign in to AWS Console
items.cause: IAM users need Console password explicitly enabled. Creating a user via CLI doesn't create a Console password by default.
items.fix: Use aws iam create-login-profile --user-name <user> --password <temp-pass> --password-reset-required. Or enable Console access in the IAM Console.

questions.question: A Lambda function has an IAM role with s3:GetObject permission. The S3 bucket has a bucket policy with an explicit Deny for the Lambda role. What happens when Lambda tries to read from S3?

options.text: Access is ALLOWED because the identity policy grants s3:GetObject
Access is DENIED because an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow
Access is ALLOWED because identity-based policies take precedence over resource-based policies
The request fails with a 500 error due to conflicting policies

questions.explanation: In IAM policy evaluation, an EXPLICIT DENY in any policy (identity, resource, SCP, or boundary) always wins — regardless of any Allow statements elsewhere. This is the #1 IAM rule to remember.

questions.question: What is the key difference between an IAM User and an IAM Role?

options.text: Users have policies; Roles do not
Users have long-lived credentials; Roles provide temporary credentials via STS
Users are for humans; Roles are only for Lambda functions
Users are regional; Roles are global

questions.explanation: Users have permanent access keys (long-lived). Roles issue temporary credentials via STS AssumeRole (1-12 hours). Roles are preferred because temporary credentials automatically expire, reducing the blast radius of a compromise. Both IAM Users and Roles are global (not regional).

questions.question: You need to allow an EC2 instance in Account A to read from an S3 bucket in Account B. What is the most secure approach?

options.text: Create an IAM user in Account B with access keys and hardcode them on the EC2 instance
Make the S3 bucket public so any account can read it
Create a cross-account IAM Role in Account B with a trust policy allowing Account A, and have the EC2 instance assume it
Share the root account credentials of Account B with Account A

questions.explanation: Cross-account IAM Roles are the gold standard. The role in Account B trusts Account A's principal. The EC2 instance (with its own role) calls AssumeRole to get temporary credentials for Account B. No long-lived keys, no public access, full audit trail in CloudTrail.

questions.question: What does a Permission Boundary do?

options.text: It restricts which AWS Regions a user can access
It sets the maximum permissions an IAM entity can have, even if their identity policy grants broader access
It replaces the need for identity-based policies
It only applies to the root account

questions.explanation: Permission Boundaries define the ceiling. If a user's identity policy allows s3:*, but their boundary only allows s3:GetObject, they can only GetObject. Used for delegation: allow developers to create roles, but limit what those roles can do.

content.title: Write a Least-Privilege IAM Policy
content.description: Create an IAM policy JSON document that allows a Lambda function to: read and write items to a specific DynamoDB table, write logs to CloudWatch, and send messages to a specific SQS queue — nothing else.
requirements: Use Version "2012-10-17"
Include separate Statement entries for each service (DynamoDB, CloudWatch Logs, SQS)
DynamoDB: Allow GetItem, PutItem, Query, UpdateItem on ONE specific table ARN
CloudWatch Logs: Allow CreateLogGroup, CreateLogStream, PutLogEvents
SQS: Allow sqs:SendMessage on ONE specific queue ARN
Do NOT use wildcards (*) for Actions — list each action explicitly
Add a Sid (Statement ID) to each statement for readability
hints: SQS: sqs:SendMessage (just this one action for sending)
Never use * for actions in a least-privilege policy

questions.question: What is the difference between IAM Users, Groups, and Roles?
questions.shortAnswer: Users are permanent identities with long-lived credentials. Groups organize Users to share policies. Roles are temporary identities assumed by services or users with auto-expiring credentials.
questions.deepExplanation: Users have access keys or passwords. Groups cannot be nested. Roles use STS to issue temporary credentials (1-12 hours) and are preferred for services like Lambda, EC2.
questions.example: A Lambda function assumes a Role to access DynamoDB. A developer is added to the "Developers" Group to inherit team permissions.
questions.commonMistake: Creating IAM Users for Lambda functions instead of using Roles.
questions.followUp: When would you use an IAM User instead of IAM Identity Center?

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege?
questions.shortAnswer: Grant only the minimum permissions required to perform a task. Default deny, then add specific Allows.
questions.deepExplanation: Use specific Actions (not *), specific Resources (ARNs), and Conditions. Review unused permissions with IAM Access Analyzer.
questions.example: Grant dynamodb:GetItem on one table instead of AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess.
questions.commonMistake: Using AdministratorAccess during development and not restricting before production.
questions.followUp: How do you identify unused permissions in a production account?

questions.question: What happens when no IAM policy matches a request?
questions.shortAnswer: Implicitly denied. IAM defaults to DENY unless there is an explicit Allow.
questions.deepExplanation: Evaluation: Explicit Deny > Explicit Allow > Implicit Deny. Deny in any policy always wins.
questions.example: User has S3 read from group, but SCP denies S3 access. SCP Deny wins.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming Allow overrides Deny. Explicit Deny always wins.
questions.followUp: How do SCPs interact with IAM policies?

questions.question: Why must you enable MFA on the root account?
questions.shortAnswer: Root has unrestricted access. MFA prevents catastrophic compromise from a stolen password.
questions.deepExplanation: Root can close the account, change support plan, enable/disable regions. No IAM user can do these. MFA adds a second factor (TOTP, FIDO2).
questions.example: Attacker gets root password from phishing. With MFA, they still cannot log in.
questions.commonMistake: Not enabling MFA on root immediately after account creation.
questions.followUp: Can you enforce MFA on IAM Users with a policy condition?

questions.question: Managed vs inline policies?
questions.shortAnswer: Managed: standalone, reusable. Inline: embedded in one entity, not reusable.
questions.deepExplanation: AWS Managed = maintained by AWS. Customer Managed = reusable across entities. Inline = deleted with entity.
questions.example: Use managed policy for team S3 access, inline for a specific Lambda role.
questions.commonMistake: Using inline policies everywhere making audit impossible.
questions.followUp: What is the max size of managed vs inline policies?

questions.question: Identity-based vs resource-based policies?
questions.shortAnswer: Identity-based: attached to Users/Groups/Roles, defines what identity CAN do. Resource-based: attached to resources, defines WHO can access.
questions.deepExplanation: Resource-based supports cross-account without AssumeRole. Same-account: union of permissions. Cross-account: BOTH must allow.
questions.example: S3 bucket policy allows Account B. Account B role also needs S3 permissions.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting cross-account requires BOTH sides to allow.
questions.followUp: Which services support resource-based policies?

questions.question: What is a trust policy?
questions.shortAnswer: A policy on an IAM Role defining which principals can assume (sts:AssumeRole) it.
questions.deepExplanation: Every Role has trust policy (who) + permission policy (what). Without trust policy allowing a principal, they cannot assume the role.
questions.example: Principal: {"Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com"} allows Lambda to assume the role.
questions.commonMistake: Editing permission policy but forgetting to update trust policy.
questions.followUp: What is ExternalId and when to use it?

questions.question: How do permission boundaries work?
questions.shortAnswer: They set MAXIMUM permissions. Effective = intersection of identity policy AND boundary.
questions.deepExplanation: Even with AdministratorAccess, boundary limits actual permissions. Enables delegation: admins can let developers create roles that never exceed certain permissions.
questions.example: Boundary allows S3 and DynamoDB only. Identity policy with EC2 permissions has no effect.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking boundaries grant permissions. They only restrict.
questions.followUp: Can you attach a boundary to a Group?

questions.question: What is IAM Access Analyzer?
questions.shortAnswer: Identifies resources shared externally and validates IAM policies against best practices.
questions.deepExplanation: Uses automated reasoning to analyze resource-based policies on S3, IAM roles, KMS, Lambda, SQS. Generates findings for resources accessible outside your zone of trust.
questions.example: Detects S3 bucket policy allowing Principal "*" — flags as publicly accessible.
questions.commonMistake: Not enabling Access Analyzer in all regions.
questions.followUp: How does it differ from AWS Config?

questions.question: Explain cross-account access with AssumeRole.
questions.shortAnswer: Account A creates Role trusting Account B. Account B calls sts:AssumeRole to get temporary credentials for Account A resources.
questions.deepExplanation: Steps: Create role with trust policy, attach permissions, call AssumeRole from other account, receive temp credentials (1-12 hrs). Use ExternalId for third parties.
questions.example: CI/CD in Dev account assumes deployment role in Prod account.
questions.commonMistake: Not using ExternalId for third-party access (confused deputy risk).
questions.followUp: What is the confused deputy problem?

questions.question: How does policy evaluation work with SCPs + permission boundaries + session policies?
questions.shortAnswer: Effective = intersection of ALL policy types. Request must be allowed by ALL: SCP AND identity AND boundary AND session AND resource. Explicit Deny in ANY wins.
questions.deepExplanation: Full chain: SCPs → Resource-based → Identity-based → Permission boundaries → Session policies. For same-account, resource-based with explicit principal can bypass identity restrictions.
questions.example: Developer has AdminAccess but SCP denies iam:CreateUser in prod OU. Cannot create users.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming SCPs are evaluated last. They restrict even root (except certain ops).
questions.followUp: Can the management account be restricted by SCPs?

questions.question: What are IAM Conditions and how to use them for fine-grained access?
questions.shortAnswer: Conditions add constraints using operators (StringEquals, IpAddress) against context keys (aws:SourceIp, aws:RequestedRegion, aws:PrincipalTag).
questions.deepExplanation: Enable ABAC. Examples: restrict to specific regions, require MFA, restrict by IP, enforce encryption, tag-based access. Multiple conditions = AND. Multiple values = OR.
questions.example: Require MFA AND specific regions: StringEquals aws:RequestedRegion + Bool aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent.
questions.commonMistake: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is absent (not false) when MFA not used.
questions.followUp: How to implement ABAC using tag conditions?

questions.question: What is iam:PassRole and why is it a security concern?
questions.shortAnswer: PassRole allows assigning a Role to a service. Without restrictions, users can escalate privileges by passing admin roles to Lambda/EC2.
questions.deepExplanation: When creating Lambda, you need iam:PassRole on the execution role. Mitigate with conditions: iam:PassedToService (limit services), Resource (limit role ARNs).
questions.example: Restrict: Allow PassRole only for roles matching "LambdaExec-*" passed only to lambda.amazonaws.com.
questions.commonMistake: Granting iam:PassRole on Resource * without conditions.
questions.followUp: What other IAM actions lead to privilege escalation?

questions.question: How do you audit unused IAM permissions at scale?
questions.shortAnswer: Use Access Analyzer policy generation from CloudTrail, Access Advisor for last-accessed timestamps, credential reports for unused keys, Config rules for compliance.
questions.deepExplanation: Strategy: Enable CloudTrail everywhere, generate policies from 90-day activity, check Access Advisor, automate key disabling with Lambda, use iam-user-unused-credentials-check rule.
questions.example: Access Analyzer shows role only used GetItem and Query. Generate policy with only those actions.
questions.commonMistake: Revoking permissions without checking quarterly batch jobs.
questions.followUp: How to implement continuous least-privilege review?

questions.question: Explain aws:SourceIp vs aws:VpcSourceIp conditions.
questions.shortAnswer: SourceIp = public IP of caller. VpcSourceIp = private IP when request goes through VPC endpoint.
questions.deepExplanation: Through VPC endpoint, SourceIp may be the endpoint's IP. VpcSourceIp is the instance's private IP. Use SourceIp for console/CLI restrictions, VpcSourceIp for VPC endpoint restrictions.
questions.example: Restrict S3 to corporate VPN: IpAddress aws:SourceIp 203.0.113.0/24.
questions.commonMistake: Using SourceIp when traffic goes through NAT Gateway — IP is NAT EIP, not instance IP.
questions.followUp: How do VPC endpoint policies interact with bucket policies?

questions.question: Developer gets AccessDenied on s3:PutObject despite having AmazonS3FullAccess. Troubleshoot.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: bucket policy Deny, SCP restrictions, permission boundary, VPC endpoint policy, S3 Block Public Access, KMS key policy.
questions.deepExplanation: Systematic: Check CloudTrail for error, run Policy Simulator, check bucket policy for Deny, check OU SCP, check KMS key policy if using CMK, check VPC endpoint policy.
questions.example: Bucket had Deny for PutObject without KMS encryption. Developer wasn't specifying SSE-KMS header.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming S3FullAccess is sufficient without checking bucket policies and SCPs.
questions.followUp: How to set up alerts for AccessDenied in CloudTrail?

questions.question: Third-party SaaS vendor needs read access to your S3 bucket. Most secure approach?
questions.shortAnswer: Create cross-account Role with ExternalId. Vendor assumes role. Never share access keys.
questions.deepExplanation: Create role trusting vendor account with ExternalId condition. Attach policy for specific bucket/actions only. Set minimum session duration. Monitor with CloudTrail.
questions.example: Trust policy with ExternalId: StringEquals sts:ExternalId vendor-abc-2024.
questions.commonMistake: Sharing IAM User access keys. Keys don't expire and leak easily.
questions.followUp: What is the confused deputy problem and how does ExternalId solve it?

questions.question: Merging acquired startup AWS account into your Organization. How to handle IAM?
questions.shortAnswer: Invite account, apply SCPs, migrate to IAM Identity Center, implement permission sets, audit with Access Analyzer. Don't delete old IAM users until SSO works.
questions.deepExplanation: Phase approach: invite + SCP → enable SSO → create permission sets → migrate users in batches → disable old users → delete after verification.
questions.example: Apply SCP denying iam:CreateUser in acquired account while migrating to SSO.
questions.commonMistake: Deleting IAM users before SSO is fully tested, causing outages.
questions.followUp: How to handle service-linked roles in Organizations?

questions.question: CloudTrail shows root account created IAM user at 3 AM. How to respond?
questions.shortAnswer: Incident response: verify if authorized, rotate root creds, delete suspicious user, check for backdoors (keys, roles, Lambda), enable root MFA, report.
questions.deepExplanation: Check created user for admin access/keys. Check for modified roles, Lambda functions, EC2 in unusual regions (crypto mining). Review billing.
questions.example: Attacker created admin user with access keys, launched EC2 for crypto mining.
questions.commonMistake: Only deleting suspicious user without checking other persistence mechanisms.
questions.followUp: How to prevent root usage with SCPs and monitoring?

questions.question: Design tag-based access control (ABAC) for 200 developers.
questions.shortAnswer: Use aws:PrincipalTag and aws:ResourceTag conditions. Tag roles with Project/Environment. Create one policy matching tags. New projects work without policy changes.
questions.deepExplanation: Define tag keys (Project, Environment, Team). Tag all IAM roles and resources. Create single policy: Allow when PrincipalTag matches ResourceTag. Scales automatically.
questions.example: Condition: aws:ResourceTag/Project equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/Project}.
questions.commonMistake: Not enforcing tag requirements at creation time.
questions.followUp: How to enforce mandatory tagging at resource creation?

questions.question: EC2 instance cannot access S3 despite role having S3 permissions.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: instance profile attached, IMDS accessible, SG allows outbound 443, bucket policy no Deny, VPC endpoint policy, NACL, IMDSv2 hop limit.
questions.deepExplanation: Common causes: no instance profile, SG/NACL blocks 443, bucket explicit deny, VPC endpoint policy restriction, IMDSv2 hop limit=1 for containers.
questions.example: VPC S3 endpoint policy only allowed company-logs-* buckets, instance tried company-data-prod.
questions.commonMistake: Only checking IAM role without checking VPC endpoint and network config.
questions.followUp: How to troubleshoot metadata service issues?

questions.question: After key rotation, application stops working.
questions.shortAnswer: App using old key. Update all locations: env vars, credentials file, Secrets Manager, CI/CD, containers. Don't delete old key until new one is confirmed working.
questions.deepExplanation: Safe rotation: create new key (user has 2), update all locations, test, make old inactive, monitor 24-48h, then delete old.
questions.example: ECS task definition had old key hardcoded. Updated and redeployed.
questions.commonMistake: Deleting old key immediately before confirming all apps updated.
questions.followUp: How to automate key rotation with Lambda and Secrets Manager?

questions.question: Policy Simulator shows Allow but actual call returns AccessDenied.
questions.shortAnswer: Simulator only checks identity policies. Doesn't check SCPs, resource-based Deny, VPC endpoint policies, session policies, permission boundaries.
questions.deepExplanation: Real requests go through full chain: SCPs → boundaries → session → identity → resource → endpoint. Any Deny blocks. Use CloudTrail for actual error reason.
questions.example: Simulator showed Allow for PutObject, but OU SCP denied S3 writes in prod.
questions.commonMistake: Relying solely on Policy Simulator for access testing.
questions.followUp: What tools show complete effective permissions?

questions.question: Lambda returns "security token expired" error.
questions.shortAnswer: Code is caching STS credentials beyond expiration. If calling AssumeRole, do it inside handler, not at module level. Lambda auto-refreshes execution role creds.
questions.deepExplanation: Lambda provides fresh creds via execution role. But if code calls AssumeRole at module level and caches in global variable, warm containers reuse stale tokens after 1h.
questions.example: Developer put AssumeRole at import time. First invocation worked, but warm containers used expired tokens.
questions.commonMistake: Initializing AssumeRole at module level without refresh logic.
questions.followUp: How to configure STS session duration for Lambda?

questions.question: New IAM policy changes not taking effect.
questions.shortAnswer: IAM is eventually consistent (seconds to propagate). Also check: policy attached to correct entity, valid JSON (typos in ARNs/actions), existing sessions use old cached credentials.
questions.deepExplanation: IAM replicates globally, usually seconds, rarely up to a minute. STS tokens embed permissions at issuance — policy changes don't affect existing tokens. Must re-authenticate.
questions.example: Updated role policy but Lambda kept AccessDenied. Redeployed function (new container) fixed it.
questions.commonMistake: Typo in action name (s3:Getobject vs s3:GetObject) silently fails.
questions.followUp: How long do STS temp creds remain valid?

title: Amazon S3 — Store Files & Static Assets
description: Object storage: buckets, storage classes, versioning, lifecycle policies, pre-signed URLs, and event notifications.
subtitle: Amazon S3 — Simple Storage Service
objectives: Create and configure S3 buckets with proper security settings
Choose the right storage class based on access patterns and cost
Implement versioning and lifecycle policies for data management
Secure buckets using bucket policies, ACLs, and Block Public Access
Generate pre-signed URLs for temporary object access
Configure S3 event notifications to trigger Lambda functions
Host a static website on S3 with CloudFront distribution

content.html:
🪣
The Universal Storage Layer of AWS
S3 stores over 100 trillion objects. Every AWS service uses S3 — CloudTrail logs, Lambda deployment packages, ELB access logs, EMR data, SageMaker datasets. It's 99.999999999% (11 nines) durable — you'd lose 1 object out of 10 billion every 10,000 years.
Storage ClassAvailabilityMin DurationUse CaseCost (per GB/mo)
S3 Standard99.99%NoneFrequently accessed data~$0.023
S3 Intelligent-Tiering99.9%NoneUnknown/changing access patterns~$0.023 + monitoring
S3 Standard-IA99.9%30 daysInfrequent but rapid access needed~$0.0125
S3 One Zone-IA99.5%30 daysRe-creatable infrequent data~$0.01
S3 Glacier Instant99.9%90 daysArchive with instant retrieval~$0.004
S3 Glacier Flexible99.99%90 daysArchive (1-12 hour retrieval)~$0.0036
S3 Glacier Deep Archive99.99%180 daysLong-term compliance (12-48hr)~$0.00099
⚠️
S3 Buckets Are Global — Names Are Unique Worldwide
Bucket names must be globally unique across ALL AWS accounts. Data is stored in a specific region, but the bucket namespace is global. Choose names carefully — once taken by anyone, no one else can use it.

nodes.label: Client App
nodes.description: Any application uploading/downloading objects: web app, mobile app, CLI, SDK, or another AWS service.

nodes.label: S3 Bucket
nodes.description: Objects stored across minimum 3 AZs (Standard). 11 nines durability. Max object size: 5 TB. Max single PUT: 5 GB (use multipart for larger).

nodes.label: S3 Event Notification
nodes.description: S3 emits events: s3:ObjectCreated:*, s3:ObjectRemoved:*, s3:LifecycleTransition. Route to Lambda, SQS, SNS, or EventBridge.

nodes.label: Lambda Processor
nodes.description: Process uploads in real-time: resize images, extract metadata, scan for viruses, index for search.

nodes.label: Lifecycle Rules
nodes.description: Automatically transition objects between storage classes or delete after expiration. Example: Standard → IA after 30 days → Glacier after 90 days → Delete after 365.

nodes.label: CloudFront CDN
nodes.description: Distribute S3 content globally via edge locations. Reduces latency, offloads S3 requests, and enables HTTPS for static websites.

content.html:
1. Bucket & Object Model

  • Bucket: Top-level container. Globally unique name. Belongs to a specific region.
  • Object: A file (up to 5 TB) stored with a key (path), metadata, and optional version ID.
  • Key: The full path including "folder" prefixes. S3 has no actual folders — images/2026/photo.jpg is just a key string.

2. Versioning

Once enabled on a bucket, every PUT overwrites the version — not the object. Deleting creates a "delete marker." You can restore any previous version. Versioning cannot be disabled, only suspended.

3. Pre-Signed URLs

Generate a time-limited URL that grants temporary access to a private object without changing bucket permissions. Ideal for: file downloads behind auth, secure uploads from browsers, sharing links that expire.

4. Server-Side Encryption

TypeKey ManagementWhen to Use
SSE-S3AWS manages keysDefault — simple, no overhead
SSE-KMSAWS KMS customer-managed keysAudit trail, key rotation, compliance
SSE-CCustomer provides keys per requestWhen you must control keys externally

5. S3 Block Public Access

Account-level and bucket-level setting that overrides any public ACLs or bucket policies. Enable at the account level as the first security measure. Turn off only for intentional public buckets (static websites).

6. Multipart Upload

Required for objects > 5 GB. Recommended for > 100 MB. Uploads parts in parallel for speed. If one part fails, only that part is retried. Remember to call CompleteMultipartUpload or AbortMultipartUpload — incomplete uploads still incur storage costs.

content.title: S3 CRUD Operations & Pre-Signed URLs

languages.label: CRUD + Pre-Signed URL
languages.code:
import boto3
import json
import os
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

s3 = boto3.client('s3')
BUCKET = os.environ.get('BUCKET_NAME', 'my-app-uploads')

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    """S3 Lambda trigger — process uploaded objects."""
    for record in event['Records']:
        bucket = record['s3']['bucket']['name']
        key    = record['s3']['object']['key']
        size   = record['s3']['object'].get('size', 0)
        event_name = record['eventName']  # e.g. ObjectCreated:Put

        logger.info("S3 event: %s | bucket=%s key=%s size=%d",
                     event_name, bucket, key, size)

        # Get the object
        response = s3.get_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key)
        content_type = response['ContentType']
        body = response['Body'].read()

        logger.info("Object type: %s, size: %d bytes", content_type, len(body))

        # Copy with new storage class
        s3.copy_object(
            CopySource={'Bucket': bucket, 'Key': key},
            Bucket=bucket,
            Key=f'processed/{key}',
            StorageClass='STANDARD_IA',
            ServerSideEncryption='aws:kms'
        )

        # Generate pre-signed URL (valid 1 hour)
        presigned_url = s3.generate_presigned_url(
            'get_object',
            Params={'Bucket': bucket, 'Key': key},
            ExpiresIn=3600  # seconds
        )
        logger.info("Pre-signed URL: %s", presigned_url)

    return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': 'Processed'}


def upload_with_metadata(file_path, key, metadata):
    """Upload a file with custom metadata."""
    s3.upload_file(
        Filename=file_path,
        Bucket=BUCKET,
        Key=key,
        ExtraArgs={
            'Metadata': metadata,
            'ServerSideEncryption': 'aws:kms',
            'StorageClass': 'INTELLIGENT_TIERING',
            'ContentType': 'application/json'
        }
    )
    logger.info("Uploaded %s to s3://%s/%s", file_path, BUCKET, key)

explanations.text: S3 Event Notification triggers Lambda with event.Records containing bucket name, object key, size, and event type.
get_object returns a streaming Body. Call .read() to get bytes. For large files, stream in chunks to avoid memory issues.
ServerSideEncryption=aws:kms uses KMS encryption. For SSE-S3, use AES256. KMS provides audit trail of key usage in CloudTrail.
Pre-signed URLs grant temporary access to private objects. The URL contains your credentials embedded — anyone with the URL can access the object until expiry.

items.title: 403 Forbidden on S3 GET request
items.error: AccessDenied when trying to read an object
items.cause: Block Public Access enabled (correct!) but you expected public access, or IAM policy missing s3:GetObject, or bucket policy has explicit deny.
items.fix: For private access: verify IAM role has s3:GetObject on the bucket ARN/*. For public website: disable Block Public Access AND add a bucket policy allowing s3:GetObject to Principal "*".

items.title: Incomplete Multipart Upload consuming storage
items.error: S3 costs increasing without new uploads
items.cause: Multipart uploads that were started but never completed (AbortMultipartUpload never called). Each incomplete upload stores uploaded parts.
items.fix: Add a lifecycle rule: AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload with DaysAfterInitiation: 7. This auto-cleans abandoned uploads.

items.title: S3 event triggers Lambda twice
items.error: Lambda processes the same S3 upload event multiple times
items.cause: S3 event notifications are at-least-once delivery. Lambda may be invoked more than once for the same event.
items.fix: Make your Lambda idempotent. Use the S3 object ETag or version ID as an idempotency key. Check DynamoDB for existing records before processing.

items.title: Static website returns 404 for routes
items.error: SPA routes return 404 after page refresh
items.cause: S3 static hosting serves files by key path. /about maps to a key named "about" which doesn't exist as a file.
items.fix: Set the Error Document to index.html in S3 static hosting config. Or use CloudFront with a custom error response that returns index.html for 404s.

questions.question: You need to store log files that are accessed daily for the first 30 days, rarely accessed for the next 60 days, and must be retained for 7 years for compliance. What S3 strategy should you use?

options.text: Store everything in S3 Standard forever
S3 Standard → Lifecycle to Standard-IA at 30 days → Glacier Deep Archive at 90 days → Delete at 2555 days
Store directly in Glacier Deep Archive from day 1
Use S3 One Zone-IA for everything

questions.explanation: Lifecycle policies automate storage class transitions based on age. Standard for active access (30 days), Standard-IA for infrequent (30-90), Glacier Deep Archive for long-term compliance (cheapest). Delete after retention period. This optimizes cost while meeting access and compliance needs.

questions.question: What is the maximum size of a single S3 object, and how do you upload files larger than 5 GB?

options.text: 5 GB max. Cannot upload larger files.
5 TB max. Use Multipart Upload for files > 5 GB (recommended for > 100 MB).
Unlimited size. S3 handles chunking automatically.
5 TB max. Use S3 Transfer Acceleration only.

questions.explanation: S3 max object size is 5 TB. Single PUT is limited to 5 GB. For larger files, use Multipart Upload which uploads parts in parallel (max 10,000 parts, min 5 MB per part). Recommended for any file > 100 MB for faster uploads and automatic retry of individual parts.

questions.question: How does S3 achieve 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability?

options.text: S3 stores each object in a single AZ with RAID-6 disk arrays
S3 automatically replicates each object across a minimum of 3 Availability Zones within the region
S3 backs up all data to Glacier automatically
S3 uses cross-region replication by default

questions.explanation: S3 Standard stores objects redundantly across a minimum of 3 physically separated AZs. This protects against AZ-level failures (fire, flood, power loss). Cross-region replication is NOT automatic — it must be configured explicitly for disaster recovery.

questions.question: What are S3 storage classes and when to use each?
questions.shortAnswer: Standard (frequent access), IA (infrequent, fast retrieval), One Zone-IA (single AZ, cheaper), Glacier Instant (ms retrieval), Glacier Flexible (min-hrs), Deep Archive (12-48h).
questions.deepExplanation: All classes have 11 9s durability. Standard: 99.99% availability. IA: retrieval fee per GB. Intelligent-Tiering: auto-moves between tiers based on access patterns.
questions.commonMistake: Storing frequently accessed data in Glacier, causing high retrieval costs.
questions.followUp: How does Intelligent-Tiering work?

questions.question: How does S3 versioning work?
questions.shortAnswer: Keeps all versions of an object. Each upload creates a new version. Deletes add a delete marker. Previous versions are recoverable.
questions.deepExplanation: Once enabled, cannot be disabled (only suspended). Each version has unique ID. Storage costs include all versions. Use lifecycle rules to expire old versions.
questions.commonMistake: Not using lifecycle rules to delete old versions, causing unbounded costs.
questions.followUp: What happens when versioning is suspended?

questions.question: What is a pre-signed URL?
questions.shortAnswer: Time-limited URL granting temporary access to a private S3 object without AWS credentials.
questions.deepExplanation: Contains signature, expiration, permissions. For GET or PUT. Max 7 days with IAM user. Generated server-side.
questions.commonMistake: Setting very long expiration times, reducing security.
questions.followUp: What if the generating credentials are revoked?

questions.question: What is S3 Block Public Access?
questions.shortAnswer: Safety net preventing accidental public exposure. Account and bucket-level settings override public grants in policies/ACLs.
questions.deepExplanation: Four settings: BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets. Account-level overrides bucket-level.
questions.commonMistake: Disabling account-level BPA to make one bucket public, exposing all buckets.
questions.followUp: Can you make a bucket public with BPA enabled?

questions.question: Max object size in S3?
questions.shortAnswer: 5 TB per object. Single PUT limit 5 GB. Use multipart upload for objects over 100 MB.
questions.deepExplanation: Multipart: 5 MB to 5 GB parts, up to 10,000 parts, parallel upload. S3 Transfer Acceleration for long-distance transfers.
questions.commonMistake: Not using multipart for large files, causing timeouts.
questions.followUp: How does Transfer Acceleration work?

questions.question: Explain S3 event notifications.
questions.shortAnswer: Trigger Lambda, SQS, SNS, or EventBridge on object create/delete/restore. Use for real-time processing pipelines.
questions.deepExplanation: Events: ObjectCreated:*, ObjectRemoved:*, ObjectRestore:*. Filter by prefix/suffix. One destination per event per prefix unless using EventBridge.
questions.commonMistake: Creating recursive triggers (Lambda writes to same bucket).
questions.followUp: How to prevent recursive Lambda invocations?

questions.question: S3 replication: SRR vs CRR?
questions.shortAnswer: SRR: Same-Region for compliance/aggregation. CRR: Cross-Region for DR/latency. Both require versioning, replicate new objects only.
questions.deepExplanation: Not retroactive — use Batch Replication for existing. Can replicate cross-account with ownership override. Supports encrypted objects with KMS key configuration.
questions.commonMistake: Expecting existing objects to replicate automatically.
questions.followUp: How to replicate existing objects?

questions.question: Server-side encryption options?
questions.shortAnswer: SSE-S3 (AWS-managed, default), SSE-KMS (KMS with audit trail), SSE-C (customer-provided keys). All encrypt at rest.
questions.deepExplanation: SSE-S3: AES-256, zero config. SSE-KMS: CloudTrail logging, key policies, S3 Bucket Key reduces KMS costs. SSE-C: you provide key per request, AWS doesn't store it.
questions.commonMistake: Using SSE-C without proper key management — lose key = lose data.
questions.followUp: What is S3 Bucket Key and how does it reduce KMS costs?

questions.question: What is S3 Object Lock?
questions.shortAnswer: WORM protection. Governance mode: override with special permissions. Compliance mode: nobody can delete, not even root.
questions.deepExplanation: Requires versioning. Legal Hold: indefinite lock independent of retention. Compliance mode retention is immutable.
questions.commonMistake: Enabling Compliance mode in testing — truly immutable until retention expires.
questions.followUp: Object Lock vs Glacier Vault Lock?

questions.question: What are S3 access points?
questions.shortAnswer: Named endpoints with dedicated access policies. Simplify managing access for different teams to shared data.
questions.deepExplanation: Each has own DNS, policy, network controls (VPC/internet). Bucket can have thousands. Delegates management from one complex bucket policy to multiple simple ones.
questions.commonMistake: Not restricting access points to VPC-only for sensitive data.
questions.followUp: How do access points simplify data lake access?

questions.question: Optimize S3 for high request rates?
questions.shortAnswer: Auto-scales to 3,500 PUT and 5,500 GET per prefix per second. Use random prefixes, multipart upload, Transfer Acceleration, byte-range fetches.
questions.deepExplanation: Partition key is object key prefix. Distribute across prefixes. CloudFront for reads. S3 Select for querying inside objects.
questions.commonMistake: Sequential date prefixes (2024/01/01/) causing partition hotspots.
questions.followUp: How does S3 Select reduce costs?

questions.question: Design a cost-efficient data lake on S3?
questions.shortAnswer: Intelligent-Tiering, lifecycle rules, Parquet/ORC formats, partitioning by date, compression, S3 analytics for tier recommendations.
questions.deepExplanation: Raw → Standard, processed → IA after 30d, archive → Glacier after 90d. Columnar formats reduce Athena scan costs 90%. Glue Data Catalog for metadata.
questions.commonMistake: CSV without partitioning = full table scans = 100x cost.
questions.followUp: How to calculate Athena query costs by format?

questions.question: Explain S3 batch operations.
questions.shortAnswer: Process billions of objects: copy, invoke Lambda, restore, tag, ACL, Object Lock. Uses manifest from Inventory or CSV.
questions.deepExplanation: Components: manifest + operation + IAM role. Tracks progress, retries failures. Integrates with S3 Inventory.
questions.commonMistake: Running batch ops without testing on small subset first.
questions.followUp: How to generate manifest from S3 Inventory?

questions.question: What is S3 Storage Lens?
questions.shortAnswer: Org-wide analytics: storage usage, activity metrics, cost optimization recommendations across all buckets.
questions.deepExplanation: Free: 28 metrics, 14 days. Advanced: 35+ metrics, 15 months, CloudWatch publishing. Identifies: incomplete multipart uploads, non-current versions, missing lifecycle rules.
questions.commonMistake: Not enabling advanced metrics for activity-based insights.
questions.followUp: How to set up Storage Lens across an Organization?

questions.question: S3 Glacier Vault Lock vs Object Lock?
questions.shortAnswer: Vault Lock: vault-level WORM for Glacier archives, irreversible once completed. Object Lock: object-level for S3 buckets, flexible modes.
questions.deepExplanation: Vault Lock: 24-hour abort window then irreversible. Designed for SEC/CFTC/FINRA compliance. Different services, different granularity.
questions.commonMistake: Completing Vault Lock in test environment — truly irreversible.
questions.followUp: Design compliant archival using both?

questions.question: S3 costs jumped 300%. How to investigate?
questions.shortAnswer: Cost Explorer → S3 usage type, Storage Lens → bucket growth, check versioning without lifecycle, incomplete multipart uploads, unexpected external access, replication costs.
questions.deepExplanation: Don't just check storage — request costs (LIST/GET) can spike. Check for bots scanning public buckets.
questions.commonMistake: Only looking at storage costs, ignoring request costs.
questions.followUp: How to set up S3 request-level CloudWatch metrics?

questions.question: Design secure file sharing for 500 external partners.
questions.shortAnswer: Access points per partner, pre-signed URLs for time-limited access, CloudFront signed URLs, Cognito auth, malware scanning Lambda.
questions.deepExplanation: Partner-specific prefix, staging → scan → approved pipeline. All access logged in CloudTrail and S3 logs.
questions.commonMistake: Public bucket policies instead of pre-signed URLs.
questions.followUp: How to implement virus scanning for uploads?

questions.question: Migrate 50 TB on-prem to S3?
questions.shortAnswer: DataSync over Direct Connect for ongoing sync, Snowball Edge for one-time if bandwidth limited, Transfer Acceleration for internet.
questions.deepExplanation: 50 TB over 1 Gbps ≈ 5 days. Over 100 Mbps ≈ 50 days → use Snowball. Verify with checksums.
questions.commonMistake: Using simple s3 cp — no resume, no parallelism, no throttling.
questions.followUp: When to choose Snowball vs DataSync vs Transfer Acceleration?

questions.question: Prove to auditor no S3 data modified in past year?
questions.shortAnswer: Object Lock compliance mode, CloudTrail logs, S3 versioning, MFA Delete, S3 Inventory with checksums.
questions.deepExplanation: Object Lock prevents modification, CloudTrail proves who did what, versioning preserves all versions, MFA Delete prevents version deletion.
questions.commonMistake: Only CloudTrail without Object Lock — proves WHO but doesn't prevent WHAT.
questions.followUp: How to meet SEC 17a-4 with S3?

questions.question: Process 10,000 image uploads per second?
questions.shortAnswer: Random hash prefixes, S3 events → SQS → Lambda (SQS as buffer), processed images → CloudFront-backed bucket.
questions.deepExplanation: S3: 3,500 PUTs per prefix. 3 prefixes = 10,500. SQS provides buffering vs direct Lambda invocation which can hit concurrency limits.
questions.commonMistake: Direct Lambda trigger at this scale hits concurrency limits. Use SQS buffer.
questions.followUp: How to handle S3 event delivery failures?

questions.question: 403 Forbidden accessing S3 object despite bucket policy allowing your role.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: object-level ACL, Block Public Access, VPC endpoint policy, KMS key policy, cross-account object ownership.
questions.deepExplanation: Cross-account: uploader owns object, bucket owner can't access unless ACL grants bucket-owner-full-control or BucketOwnerEnforced is set.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting object ownership in cross-account scenarios.
questions.followUp: What is BucketOwnerEnforced?

questions.question: S3 replication not working for new objects.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: versioning on both buckets, replication role permissions, KMS key policy, rule status, filter matching.
questions.deepExplanation: KMS objects need kms:Decrypt on source key + kms:Encrypt on destination key in replication role.
questions.commonMistake: Expecting existing objects to replicate. Use Batch Replication.
questions.followUp: How to monitor replication lag?

questions.question: Lifecycle rule not transitioning objects.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: rule enabled, filter matches, 30-day minimum for IA, objects must be >128 KB for IA, runs asynchronously.
questions.deepExplanation: Objects <128 KB skip IA/One Zone-IA transition. Cannot go IA→Standard. Check Storage Lens for effectiveness.
questions.commonMistake: Expecting immediate transition — 30-day minimum for IA.
questions.followUp: How to audit lifecycle effectiveness with Storage Lens?

questions.question: Multipart upload failing with EntityTooSmall.
questions.shortAnswer: Each part except last must be ≥5 MB. Set lifecycle rule to auto-abort incomplete multipart uploads.
questions.deepExplanation: Constraints: 5 MB min part, 5 GB max part, 10,000 max parts, 5 TB max object. Incomplete uploads still incur storage costs.
questions.commonMistake: No lifecycle rule for incomplete uploads = orphaned parts = hidden costs.
questions.followUp: How to clean up incomplete multipart uploads?

questions.question: S3 Select returning empty results.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: format spec matches actual (CSV/JSON/Parquet), compression type, column names case-sensitive, SQL syntax. Test with SELECT * LIMIT 1.
questions.deepExplanation: Common: specifying CSV but file is JSON, missing header row config, wrong compression codec, SSE-C not supported.
questions.commonMistake: Not setting FileHeaderInfo:USE for CSV with headers.
questions.followUp: S3 Select vs Athena for queries?

content.title: EC2 Instance in a VPC with Security Groups & EBS

nodes.label: Internet
nodes.description: Public internet traffic hits the EC2 instance via its public IP or Elastic IP.

nodes.label: Internet Gateway
nodes.description: Internet Gateway allows communication between instances in the VPC and the internet.

nodes.label: Security Group
nodes.description: Stateful firewall at the instance level. Rules define allowed inbound/outbound traffic by protocol, port, and source. Default: deny all inbound, allow all outbound.

nodes.label: EC2 Instance
nodes.description: Virtual server running your AMI. Attached to a subnet (public or private). Has an instance profile (IAM role) for AWS API access.

nodes.label: EBS Volume
nodes.description: Block storage volumes attached to EC2. Persist independently from the instance lifecycle. Support encryption (KMS), snapshots, and different types (gp3, io2, st1).

nodes.label: Instance Profile
nodes.description: IAM role attached to EC2 via Instance Profile. Provides temporary credentials automatically — no access keys needed on the instance.

content.html:
1. AMI (Amazon Machine Image)

A template containing the OS, application server, and applications. Launch multiple identical instances from one AMI. You can create custom AMIs from running instances (golden images).

2. Security Groups (Stateful Firewall)

Key principle: Security Groups are STATEFUL — if inbound traffic is allowed, the response is automatically allowed (no outbound rule needed for responses).

  • Default: ALL inbound denied, ALL outbound allowed
  • Rules are ALLOW only — you cannot create DENY rules
  • Reference other SGs as source: "Allow inbound from the ALB security group"

3. Key Pairs

SSH key pairs for Linux instance access. AWS stores the public key, you keep the private key. For Windows, use the key pair to decrypt the admin password. Best practice: Use SSM Session Manager instead of SSH for production access.

4. EBS Volume Types

TypeIOPSThroughputUse Case
gp33,000 - 16,000125 - 1,000 MB/sGeneral purpose (default choice)
io2 Block ExpressUp to 256,000Up to 4,000 MB/sMission-critical databases
st1N/AUp to 500 MB/sBig data, log processing (sequential)
sc1N/AUp to 250 MB/sCold storage (lowest cost)

5. Instance Metadata Service (IMDS v2)

HTTP endpoint at 169.254.169.254 providing instance info (ID, region, IAM role credentials). Always use IMDSv2 (requires session token) — IMDSv1 is vulnerable to SSRF attacks.

6. User Data

Bootstrap script that runs at first launch. Use for installing software, configuring services, pulling code from S3. Runs as root. Limited to 16 KB.

languages.label: Launch & Manage
languages.code:
import boto3
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

ec2 = boto3.resource('ec2')
ec2_client = boto3.client('ec2')

def launch_instance(ami_id, instance_type, key_name, sg_id, subnet_id):
    """
    Launch an EC2 instance with best practices.
    """
    instances = ec2.create_instances(
        ImageId=ami_id,
        InstanceType=instance_type,
        KeyName=key_name,
        MinCount=1,
        MaxCount=1,
        SecurityGroupIds=[sg_id],
        SubnetId=subnet_id,
        # IMDSv2 required — blocks SSRF attacks
        MetadataOptions={
            'HttpTokens': 'required',       # Enforce IMDSv2
            'HttpEndpoint': 'enabled',
            'HttpPutResponseHopLimit': 1     # Prevent container breakout
        },
        # EBS volume: gp3, encrypted
        BlockDeviceMappings=[{
            'DeviceName': '/dev/xvda',
            'Ebs': {
                'VolumeSize': 20,            # 20 GB
                'VolumeType': 'gp3',
                'Encrypted': True,
                'DeleteOnTermination': True
            }
        }],
        # IAM Instance Profile for AWS API access
        IamInstanceProfile={'Name': 'EC2-S3-ReadOnly-Profile'},
        # Bootstrap script
        UserData="""#!/bin/bash
yum update -y
yum install -y httpd
systemctl start httpd
systemctl enable httpd
echo "Hello from $(hostname)" > /var/www/html/index.html
""",
        TagSpecifications=[{
            'ResourceType': 'instance',
            'Tags': [
                {'Key': 'Name', 'Value': 'web-server-01'},
                {'Key': 'Environment', 'Value': 'production'}
            ]
        }]
    )

    instance = instances[0]
    instance.wait_until_running()
    instance.reload()

    logger.info("Instance %s running. Public IP: %s",
                instance.id, instance.public_ip_address)
    return instance.id


def stop_instances_by_tag(tag_key, tag_value):
    """Stop all instances matching a tag (cost savings)."""
    filters = [{'Name': f'tag:{tag_key}', 'Values': [tag_value]},
               {'Name': 'instance-state-name', 'Values': ['running']}]

    instances = ec2.instances.filter(Filters=filters)
    ids = [i.id for i in instances]

    if ids:
        ec2_client.stop_instances(InstanceIds=ids)
        logger.info("Stopped %d instances: %s", len(ids), ids)
    return ids

explanations.text: MetadataOptions enforces IMDSv2. HttpTokens=required means the instance MUST use a session token to access metadata — blocks SSRF attacks that exploit IMDSv1.
gp3 is the default and most cost-effective EBS type. Always enable encryption. DeleteOnTermination=True cleans up when the instance terminates.
Instance Profile wraps an IAM Role. The instance gets temporary credentials automatically via IMDS — no hardcoded access keys.
UserData is a bootstrap script that runs once at first launch as root. Use it for initial software installation and config.

items.title: Cannot SSH to instance
items.cause: Security Group doesn't allow inbound TCP 22 from your IP, or instance is in a private subnet without a NAT/bastion, or NACL blocking.
items.fix: Check: 1) SG has port 22 open to your IP. 2) Instance has a public IP or Elastic IP. 3) Subnet route table has a route to the Internet Gateway. 4) NACL allows port 22.

items.title: Instance stuck in "stopping" state
items.error: Instance state shows "stopping" for extended period
items.cause: Underlying hardware issue or the instance is performing a large disk flush.
items.fix: Wait 10-15 minutes. If still stuck, try force-stop: aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-xxx --force. If that fails, contact AWS Support.

items.title: EBS volume full — instance unresponsive
items.error: Cannot SSH, application errors, disk full
items.cause: Root EBS volume (/dev/xvda) ran out of space. Logs, temp files, or application data filled the disk.
items.fix: Stop instance → modify volume size (aws ec2 modify-volume) → start instance → extend filesystem (growpart + resize2fs/xfs_growfs). Add CloudWatch alarm for disk usage > 80%.

items.title: Spot Instance terminated unexpectedly
items.cause: Spot price exceeded your max bid, or AWS reclaimed capacity. Spot instances can be interrupted with 2-minute warning.
items.fix: Use Spot Fleet with multiple instance types and AZs. Handle interruption via EC2 metadata (169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/spot/instance-action). Design for fault tolerance.

questions.question: An EC2 Security Group has NO inbound rules and the default outbound rule (allow all). You add an inbound rule allowing TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Can the instance respond to HTTPS requests?

options.text: No — you also need an outbound rule for TCP 443
Yes — Security Groups are stateful, so the response is automatically allowed
No — 0.0.0.0/0 only allows IPv4, not IPv6
Yes, but only from within the VPC

questions.explanation: Security Groups are STATEFUL. If inbound traffic is allowed by a rule, the response traffic is automatically allowed regardless of outbound rules. This is the key difference from NACLs (which are stateless).

questions.question: Your production web server runs 24/7 with predictable traffic. Dev instances run 8 hours/day on weekdays. What is the most cost-effective purchasing strategy?

options.text: On-Demand for everything
Reserved Instance (1yr) for production + On-Demand for dev
Spot Instances for production + Reserved for dev
Reserved for everything

questions.explanation: Production (24/7 steady state) = Reserved Instance for up to 72% savings. Dev (irregular usage) = On-Demand for flexibility (only pay when running). Never use Spot for production workloads that can't tolerate interruption.

questions.question: Why should you enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) on all EC2 instances?

options.text: IMDSv2 is faster than IMDSv1
IMDSv1 is vulnerable to SSRF attacks that can steal IAM role credentials from the metadata endpoint
IMDSv2 provides more metadata fields
IMDSv1 doesn't support IAM roles

questions.explanation: The Capital One breach (2019) exploited IMDSv1 via SSRF. IMDSv1 uses a simple GET request to 169.254.169.254 — any code running on the instance (including SSRF-exploited web apps) can steal IAM credentials. IMDSv2 requires a session token from a PUT request first, blocking SSRF attacks.

questions.question: What are EC2 instance types and how to choose?
questions.shortAnswer: Instance types define CPU, memory, storage, and network. Families: General (T/M), Compute (C), Memory (R/X), Storage (I/D), Accelerated (P/G). Choose based on workload profile.
questions.commonMistake: Using general-purpose instances for memory-intensive workloads like Redis/SAP.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between T3 burstable and M5 general purpose?

questions.question: What is the difference between EBS and instance store?
questions.shortAnswer: EBS: persistent network-attached storage, survives instance stop/restart. Instance store: ephemeral local storage, data lost on stop/terminate. Use EBS for databases, instance store for temp cache.
questions.commonMistake: Storing important data on instance store volumes.
questions.followUp: When would you use instance store instead of EBS?

questions.question: On-Demand vs Reserved vs Spot pricing?
questions.shortAnswer: On-Demand: pay per second, no commitment. Reserved: 1-3 year commitment, up to 72% discount. Spot: unused capacity, up to 90% discount but can be interrupted with 2-min notice.
questions.commonMistake: Using On-Demand for stable production workloads instead of Reserved Instances.
questions.followUp: What are Savings Plans vs Reserved Instances?

questions.question: What is a security group?
questions.shortAnswer: Virtual firewall for EC2 instances. Stateful (return traffic auto-allowed). Rules: allow only (no deny). Default: deny all inbound, allow all outbound.
questions.commonMistake: Opening port 22 (SSH) to 0.0.0.0/0 in production.
questions.followUp: Security groups vs NACLs?

questions.question: What is user data?
questions.shortAnswer: Script that runs automatically on first boot of an EC2 instance. Used to install software, configure settings, download code. Runs as root.
questions.commonMistake: Putting secrets in user data — it is visible in instance metadata.
questions.followUp: User data vs cfn-init for bootstrapping?

questions.question: How does EC2 placement groups work?
questions.shortAnswer: Three strategies: Cluster (low latency, same rack), Spread (max 7 instances/AZ, separate hardware), Partition (large distributed workloads like Hadoop/Kafka).
questions.commonMistake: Using cluster placement across AZs — cluster is single-AZ only.
questions.followUp: When would you use Partition vs Spread?

questions.question: Explain EC2 hibernation.
questions.shortAnswer: Saves RAM contents to EBS root volume before stopping. On start, RAM is restored — much faster than cold boot. Instance maintains same ID, IP, and attached volumes.
questions.commonMistake: Trying to hibernate instances with more than 150 GB RAM or instances running more than 60 days.
questions.followUp: What are the prerequisites for EC2 hibernation?

questions.question: What is an Elastic IP?
questions.shortAnswer: Static public IPv4 address. Persists across stop/start. Free when attached to running instance. Charged when unattached or attached to stopped instance.
questions.commonMistake: Not releasing unattached Elastic IPs — they incur charges.
questions.followUp: Why should you prefer DNS names over Elastic IPs?

questions.question: What are EBS volume types?
questions.shortAnswer: gp3/gp2 (general SSD), io2/io1 (provisioned IOPS SSD), st1 (throughput HDD), sc1 (cold HDD). gp3 is default. io2 for databases needing >16K IOPS.
questions.commonMistake: Using gp2 for high-IOPS database workloads — IOPS are linked to volume size in gp2.
questions.followUp: How does gp3 differ from gp2 in IOPS provisioning?

questions.question: Explain EC2 instance metadata and IMDS.
questions.shortAnswer: Metadata service at 169.254.169.254 provides instance info (ID, IP, role credentials, user data). IMDSv2 requires session token (PUT request first). Always use IMDSv2 for security.
questions.commonMistake: Not enforcing IMDSv2 — IMDSv1 is vulnerable to SSRF attacks.
questions.followUp: How does IMDSv2 prevent SSRF attacks?

questions.question: Design a cost-optimized EC2 architecture for a web application?
questions.shortAnswer: Mix of Reserved (baseline) + Spot (scaling) behind ALB. Auto Scaling Group with mixed instances policy. Graviton (ARM) instances for 20% cost savings. Right-size using Compute Optimizer.
questions.commonMistake: Not using Graviton instances — they provide better price/performance for most workloads.
questions.followUp: How do you handle Spot interruptions in a web application?

questions.question: What is EC2 Nitro System?
questions.shortAnswer: AWS custom hardware+firmware for EC2. Offloads networking, storage, security to dedicated hardware. Enables bare-metal instances, higher performance, and enhanced security (Nitro Enclaves).
questions.commonMistake: Not understanding that older non-Nitro instances have lower network and EBS performance limits.
questions.followUp: What are Nitro Enclaves and when would you use them?

questions.question: Explain EBS Multi-Attach.
questions.shortAnswer: io2 volumes can be attached to up to 16 Nitro instances simultaneously in the same AZ. For clustered applications that manage concurrent write operations. Requires cluster-aware filesystem.
questions.commonMistake: Using Multi-Attach with standard filesystems like ext4 — requires cluster-aware FS like GFS2.
questions.followUp: What are alternatives to Multi-Attach for shared storage?

questions.question: How do EC2 Capacity Reservations work?
questions.shortAnswer: Reserve capacity in a specific AZ for any duration. Guarantees instance launch even during capacity shortages. On-Demand Capacity Reservations (ODCR) with no term commitment. Can combine with Reserved Instances for cost savings.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing Capacity Reservations with Reserved Instances — CRs guarantee capacity but don't provide discounts alone.
questions.followUp: How do Capacity Reservations interact with Auto Scaling?

questions.question: What is EC2 Fleet?
questions.shortAnswer: Launch and manage fleet of On-Demand, Reserved, and Spot instances across instance types and AZs with a single API call. Defines target capacity and allocation strategy.
questions.commonMistake: Not diversifying instance types in Spot fleets — single type increases interruption risk.
questions.followUp: How does capacity-optimized allocation strategy reduce Spot interruptions?

questions.question: Your EC2 instance is unreachable via SSH. Troubleshoot.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: security group allows port 22 from your IP, NACL allows inbound 22 and outbound ephemeral ports, instance is running (not stopped/terminated), key pair matches, public IP exists, route table has IGW route.
questions.commonMistake: Only checking security group without verifying NACL and route table.
questions.followUp: How do you access an instance if you lost the SSH key?

questions.question: An EC2 instance shows "InsufficientInstanceCapacity" error. What to do?
questions.shortAnswer: Wait and retry, try different instance type, try different AZ, use On-Demand Capacity Reservation, switch to similar instance family (e.g., m5 → m5a), use EC2 Fleet with diversified types.
questions.commonMistake: Only retrying the same instance type in the same AZ.
questions.followUp: How do Capacity Reservations prevent this issue?

questions.question: Design a highly available EC2 architecture for a stateful application.
questions.shortAnswer: Multi-AZ ASG, EBS volumes with regular snapshots, ALB health checks, shared state in ElastiCache/RDS, session stickiness if needed, EFS for shared filesystem.
questions.commonMistake: Relying on local EBS for state without replication — EBS is AZ-specific.
questions.followUp: How do you handle failover for EBS-dependent applications?

questions.question: Your Spot instances keep getting interrupted. How to improve stability?
questions.shortAnswer: Diversify across 10+ instance types and all AZs. Use capacity-optimized allocation. Implement graceful shutdown handling (2-min warning). Use Spot placement score to find best regions.
questions.commonMistake: Using a single instance type for Spot — diversification is the key to reducing interruptions.
questions.followUp: How do you implement graceful Spot interruption handling?

questions.question: Reduce EC2 costs by 40% without changing architecture.
questions.shortAnswer: Right-size with Compute Optimizer, convert to Graviton (ARM), purchase Reserved/Savings Plans for baseline, Spot for variable workloads, stop dev/test instances off-hours, use latest generation instances.
questions.commonMistake: Buying 3-year Reserved Instances without usage data — workloads may change.
questions.followUp: How do Compute Optimizer recommendations work?

questions.question: EC2 instance stuck in "stopping" state.
questions.shortAnswer: Wait up to 10-15 minutes. If still stuck, force-stop via CLI: aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-xxx --force. If force-stop fails, contact AWS Support.
questions.commonMistake: Immediately terminating the instance instead of waiting or force-stopping.
questions.followUp: What causes instances to get stuck in stopping state?

questions.question: EBS volume performance is degraded.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: volume type and provisioned IOPS, CloudWatch VolumeQueueLength (>1 = contention), burst balance for gp2 (BurstBalance metric), throughput limit, instance EBS bandwidth limit.
questions.commonMistake: Not checking instance-level EBS bandwidth limits — smaller instances cap EBS throughput.
questions.followUp: How does EBS burst balance work for gp2 volumes?

questions.question: EC2 instance fails status checks.
questions.shortAnswer: System status check failure: AWS infrastructure issue → stop and start instance (migrates to new host). Instance status check failure: OS/software issue → check console output, reboot, or recreate.
questions.commonMistake: Rebooting for system check failures — you need stop/start to migrate to new hardware.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between reboot and stop/start?

questions.question: Cannot attach additional EBS volume to instance.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: volume and instance must be in same AZ, instance device limit not exceeded, volume is not attached elsewhere (unless io2 Multi-Attach). Detach from other instance first.
questions.commonMistake: Trying to attach a volume from us-east-1a to an instance in us-east-1b.
questions.followUp: How to move an EBS volume between AZs?

questions.question: EC2 instance cannot reach the internet.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: public IP or Elastic IP assigned, route table has 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW route, IGW is attached to VPC, security group allows outbound, NACL allows outbound. Private subnet: needs NAT Gateway.
questions.commonMistake: Missing the IGW route in the route table — most common cause.
questions.followUp: How does NAT Gateway enable internet access for private instances?
