Troubleshoot connectivity issues using VPC Flow Logs and Reachability Analyzer

content.html:
🏗️
Your Private Data Center in the Cloud
VPC is a logically isolated network within AWS where you control IP ranges, subnets, route tables, and gateways. Every AWS resource that needs a network (EC2, RDS, Lambda, ELB) lives inside a VPC. You cannot skip VPC — it's the foundation of all cloud networking.

Network Tiers

TierSubnet TypeInternet AccessResources
Public TierPublic subnet (route to IGW)Full inbound + outboundALB, NAT Gateway, Bastion hosts
Application TierPrivate subnet (route to NAT)Outbound only (via NAT)EC2 app servers, Lambda in VPC, ECS tasks
Data TierPrivate subnet (no internet)NoneRDS, ElastiCache, DynamoDB VPC Endpoint
⚠️
CIDR Blocks Cannot Be Changed After Creation
Plan your VPC CIDR carefully. Use /16 for production VPCs (65,536 IPs). Avoid overlapping CIDRs if you plan to peer VPCs or connect to on-premises. Secondary CIDRs can be added but the primary cannot change.

nodes.label: Internet
nodes.description: Public internet traffic.

nodes.label: Internet Gateway
nodes.description: Attaches to VPC. Provides a target in route tables for internet-routable traffic. One per VPC. Horizontally scaled, redundant, and HA.

nodes.label: ALB (Public Subnet)
nodes.description: Application Load Balancer in public subnets. Receives internet traffic on port 443, distributes to app tier in private subnets.

nodes.label: NAT Gateway
nodes.description: Allows instances in private subnets to reach the internet (for updates, API calls) while blocking inbound connections. Deployed in public subnet. ~$32/month + data processing.

nodes.label: App Server (Private)
nodes.description: EC2/ECS in private subnet. No public IP. Receives traffic only from ALB. Outbound internet via NAT Gateway.

nodes.label: Lambda (Private)
nodes.description: Lambda in VPC needs NAT Gateway for internet or VPC Endpoints for AWS services. Without either, Lambda cannot call AWS APIs.

nodes.label: RDS (Data Tier)
nodes.description: RDS in private subnet with no internet route. Only accessible from app tier via Security Group rules.

nodes.label: VPC Endpoint
nodes.description: Interface or Gateway endpoint. Allows private access to AWS services (S3, DynamoDB, SQS) without internet. Traffic stays on AWS backbone.

content.html:
1. Subnets & CIDR

Each subnet maps to ONE Availability Zone. AWS reserves 5 IPs per subnet (first 4 + last 1).

VPC:     10.0.0.0/16     (65,536 IPs)
├─ Public:  10.0.1.0/24  (251 usable)  AZ-a
├─ Public:  10.0.2.0/24  (251 usable)  AZ-b
├─ Private: 10.0.10.0/24 (251 usable)  AZ-a
├─ Private: 10.0.20.0/24 (251 usable)  AZ-b
├─ Data:    10.0.100.0/24 (251 usable) AZ-a
└─ Data:    10.0.200.0/24 (251 usable) AZ-b

2. Route Tables

DestinationTargetMeaning
10.0.0.0/16localTraffic within VPC stays internal (always present)
0.0.0.0/0igw-xxxAll other traffic → Internet Gateway (public subnet)
0.0.0.0/0nat-xxxAll other traffic → NAT Gateway (private subnet)

3. NACL vs Security Group

FeatureSecurity GroupNACL
LevelInstance (ENI)Subnet
StateStateful (return traffic auto-allowed)Stateless (must allow return traffic explicitly)
RulesAllow onlyAllow AND Deny
EvaluationAll rules evaluated togetherRules evaluated in order (lowest number first)
DefaultDeny all inbound, Allow all outboundAllow all inbound and outbound

4. VPC Endpoints

  • Gateway Endpoint (free): S3 and DynamoDB only. Route table entry. No DNS changes needed.
  • Interface Endpoint (paid): All other AWS services. Creates an ENI in your subnet with a private IP. Uses PrivateLink.

5. VPC Peering

1:1 connection between two VPCs (same or cross-account/cross-region). CIDRs must NOT overlap. Not transitive: if A↔B and B↔C, A cannot reach C via B — must create A↔C peering separately.

languages.label: VPC Builder
languages.code:
import boto3
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

ec2 = boto3.resource('ec2')
ec2_client = boto3.client('ec2')

def create_production_vpc():
    """Create a 3-tier VPC with public and private subnets."""

    # 1. Create VPC
    vpc = ec2.create_vpc(CidrBlock='10.0.0.0/16')
    vpc.wait_until_available()
    vpc.create_tags(Tags=[{'Key': 'Name', 'Value': 'prod-vpc'}])
    logger.info("VPC created: %s", vpc.id)

    # 2. Enable DNS hostnames (required for VPC endpoints)
    ec2_client.modify_vpc_attribute(
        VpcId=vpc.id,
        EnableDnsHostnames={'Value': True}
    )

    # 3. Create Internet Gateway
    igw = ec2.create_internet_gateway()
    igw.attach_to_vpc(VpcId=vpc.id)
    igw.create_tags(Tags=[{'Key': 'Name', 'Value': 'prod-igw'}])

    # 4. Create subnets
    public_subnet_a = vpc.create_subnet(
        CidrBlock='10.0.1.0/24',
        AvailabilityZone='us-east-1a',
        TagSpecifications=[{
            'ResourceType': 'subnet',
            'Tags': [{'Key': 'Name', 'Value': 'public-a'}]
        }]
    )
    private_subnet_a = vpc.create_subnet(
        CidrBlock='10.0.10.0/24',
        AvailabilityZone='us-east-1a',
        TagSpecifications=[{
            'ResourceType': 'subnet',
            'Tags': [{'Key': 'Name', 'Value': 'private-app-a'}]
        }]
    )

    # 5. Public route table → IGW
    public_rt = vpc.create_route_table()
    public_rt.create_route(DestinationCidrBlock='0.0.0.0/0', GatewayId=igw.id)
    public_rt.associate_with_subnet(SubnetId=public_subnet_a.id)
    public_rt.create_tags(Tags=[{'Key': 'Name', 'Value': 'public-rt'}])

    # 6. NAT Gateway (in public subnet, for private subnet outbound)
    eip = ec2_client.allocate_address(Domain='vpc')
    nat = ec2_client.create_nat_gateway(
        SubnetId=public_subnet_a.id,
        AllocationId=eip['AllocationId'],
        TagSpecifications=[{
            'ResourceType': 'natgateway',
            'Tags': [{'Key': 'Name', 'Value': 'prod-nat'}]
        }]
    )
    nat_id = nat['NatGateway']['NatGatewayId']
    logger.info("NAT Gateway: %s (wait for 'available' state)", nat_id)

    # 7. Private route table → NAT
    # NOTE: Must wait for NAT to be 'available' before adding route
    # In production, use a waiter or CloudFormation/CDK
    private_rt = vpc.create_route_table()
    # private_rt.create_route(DestinationCidrBlock='0.0.0.0/0', NatGatewayId=nat_id)
    private_rt.associate_with_subnet(SubnetId=private_subnet_a.id)
    private_rt.create_tags(Tags=[{'Key': 'Name', 'Value': 'private-rt'}])

    return {
        'vpcId': vpc.id,
        'publicSubnet': public_subnet_a.id,
        'privateSubnet': private_subnet_a.id,
        'igwId': igw.id,
        'natId': nat_id
    }

explanations.text: EnableDnsHostnames is required for VPC endpoints and for EC2 instances to get public DNS names.
Public route: 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW means "all non-VPC traffic goes to the internet." The local route (10.0.0.0/16 → local) is always present.
NAT Gateway must be in a PUBLIC subnet with an Elastic IP. Private subnets route through it for outbound internet. ~$32/month fixed cost.
Private route: 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway allows outbound internet (software updates, API calls) but blocks inbound connections.

items.title: Lambda in VPC cannot call AWS APIs
items.error: Lambda timeout when calling DynamoDB, S3, or SQS from a VPC-connected function
items.cause: Lambda in a private subnet has no internet route. Without a NAT Gateway or VPC Endpoint, Lambda cannot reach AWS service endpoints.
items.fix: Option A: Add NAT Gateway in public subnet + route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT in private subnet route table. Option B (recommended): Create VPC Endpoints for the specific services (free for S3/DynamoDB Gateway endpoints).

items.title: EC2 cannot reach the internet despite public IP
items.error: Instance has public IP but cannot ping 8.8.8.8 or install packages
items.cause: Subnet route table missing 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW route. Or NACL blocking outbound traffic. Or Security Group blocking outbound.
items.fix: Check: 1) Route table has 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxx. 2) NACL allows outbound on required ports (HTTP 80, HTTPS 443) AND allows return traffic (ephemeral ports 1024-65535). 3) Security Group outbound allows the traffic.

items.title: VPC Peering connection not working
items.error: Instances in peered VPCs cannot communicate
items.cause: Route table entries not added in BOTH VPCs. VPC Peering is not transitive and requires manual route configuration.
items.fix: In VPC-A route table: add 10.1.0.0/16 → pcx-xxx. In VPC-B route table: add 10.0.0.0/16 → pcx-xxx. Also verify Security Groups allow traffic from the peered VPC CIDR.

items.title: NAT Gateway charges unexpectedly high
items.error: NAT Gateway data processing costs exceeding budget
items.cause: NAT Gateway charges $0.045/GB processed. High-volume traffic (S3 downloads, API calls) through NAT is expensive.
items.fix: Use S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint (free) instead of routing S3 traffic through NAT. Use Interface Endpoints for other high-volume services. Analyze VPC Flow Logs to identify top talkers.

questions.question: A Lambda function in a private subnet needs to write to DynamoDB. There is no NAT Gateway and no VPC Endpoints. What happens?

options.text: Lambda writes to DynamoDB successfully because DynamoDB is a managed service
Lambda times out — it cannot reach the DynamoDB endpoint without internet or a VPC Endpoint
Lambda automatically creates a temporary network path to DynamoDB
Lambda fails with an IAM permission error

questions.explanation: DynamoDB is accessed via public HTTPS endpoints. Lambda in a VPC private subnet with no internet route (NAT) and no VPC Endpoint cannot reach ANY AWS service. The most cost-effective fix is a DynamoDB Gateway VPC Endpoint (free).

questions.question: What is the key difference between a NACL and a Security Group?

options.text: NACLs are stateful; Security Groups are stateless
NACLs operate at subnet level and are stateless; Security Groups operate at instance level and are stateful
NACLs support only Allow rules; Security Groups support Allow and Deny
NACLs are free; Security Groups cost money

questions.explanation: NACLs = subnet level, stateless (must explicitly allow return traffic), support Allow AND Deny, evaluated in order. Security Groups = instance level, stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), support Allow only, all rules evaluated together.

questions.question: You have VPC-A peered with VPC-B, and VPC-B peered with VPC-C. Can instances in VPC-A communicate with VPC-C?

options.text: Yes — peering is transitive through VPC-B
No — VPC Peering is NOT transitive. You must create a separate A↔C peering connection.
Yes, but only if all three VPCs are in the same region
Yes, if VPC-B forwards the traffic (acts as a router)

questions.explanation: VPC Peering is NOT transitive. A↔B and B↔C does NOT allow A↔C. For full-mesh connectivity, use AWS Transit Gateway instead — it acts as a hub that all VPCs connect to.

content.title: VPC Network Architecture Lab
content.description: Build a production VPC with public/private subnets, NAT Gateway, and VPC peering.

steps.title: Create VPC
steps.instruction: VPC → Create VPC → CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16 → Enable DNS hostnames → Create.
steps.hint: Plan CIDR carefully — cannot be changed after creation.

steps.title: Create Subnets
steps.instruction: Create 4 subnets: 2 public (10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.2.0/24) and 2 private (10.0.3.0/24, 10.0.4.0/24) across 2 AZs.
steps.hint: Use different AZs for high availability.

steps.title: Create Internet Gateway
steps.instruction: Create IGW and attach to VPC. Update public subnet route table: 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW.
steps.hint: Enable auto-assign public IP on public subnets.

steps.title: Create NAT Gateway
steps.instruction: Create NAT Gateway in public subnet with Elastic IP. Update private subnet route table: 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT GW.
steps.expectedResult: Private instances can access internet (outbound only).
steps.hint: NAT Gateway costs $0.045/hr + data processing.

steps.title: Configure NACLs
steps.instruction: Create custom NACL for private subnets. Allow inbound from VPC CIDR only. Allow outbound to 0.0.0.0/0 on ports 443, 80.
steps.expectedResult: Private subnets have network-level access control.
steps.hint: NACLs are stateless — you must allow return traffic (ephemeral ports 1024-65535).

steps.title: Test Connectivity
steps.instruction: Launch EC2 in public subnet (SSH in). Launch EC2 in private subnet. From public instance, SSH to private instance. From private instance, curl google.com.
steps.expectedResult: Public: internet access. Private: outbound internet via NAT only.
steps.hint: Use the public instance as a bastion/jump box.

questions.question: What is a VPC?
questions.shortAnswer: Virtual Private Cloud — logically isolated network in AWS. You define IP range (CIDR), create subnets, configure route tables, and control access with security groups and NACLs.
questions.commonMistake: Not planning CIDR blocks for future VPC peering — overlapping CIDRs cannot be peered.
questions.followUp: What is the maximum CIDR block size for a VPC?

questions.question: Public subnet vs private subnet?
questions.shortAnswer: Public: route table has route to Internet Gateway. Private: no direct internet route (uses NAT for outbound). It is the route table that makes it public/private, not the subnet itself.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking subnets are inherently public or private — it depends on the route table.
questions.followUp: Can a single subnet have both public and private instances?

questions.question: Security Groups vs NACLs?
questions.shortAnswer: SG: instance-level, stateful, allow-only rules. NACL: subnet-level, stateless, allow AND deny rules. SGs are the primary firewall, NACLs are the secondary defense layer.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting NACLs are stateless — must explicitly allow return traffic on ephemeral ports.
questions.followUp: In what order are SGs and NACLs evaluated?

questions.question: What is a NAT Gateway?
questions.shortAnswer: Managed service allowing private subnet instances to access internet (outbound) while preventing inbound connections. Created in a public subnet with an Elastic IP.
questions.commonMistake: Putting NAT Gateway in a private subnet — it must be in a public subnet with IGW route.
questions.followUp: NAT Gateway vs NAT Instance?

questions.question: What is an Internet Gateway?
questions.shortAnswer: Horizontally scaled, redundant gateway allowing VPC resources to communicate with the internet. One IGW per VPC. Must be attached to VPC and referenced in route table.
questions.commonMistake: Creating IGW but forgetting to add 0.0.0.0/0 route in the route table.
questions.followUp: Does an IGW perform NAT?

questions.question: What is VPC peering?
questions.shortAnswer: Private network connection between two VPCs using AWS backbone. Non-transitive — if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming VPC peering is transitive. Each pair needs its own peering connection.
questions.followUp: When would you use Transit Gateway instead of VPC peering?

questions.question: What are VPC endpoints?
questions.shortAnswer: Private connections to AWS services without using internet. Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB — free). Interface endpoints (most other services — uses PrivateLink, has cost).
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to update route table for Gateway endpoints and security group for Interface endpoints.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between Gateway and Interface endpoints?

questions.question: What is VPC Flow Logs?
questions.shortAnswer: Captures IP traffic information for network interfaces in VPC. Publish to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Kinesis. Used for monitoring, troubleshooting, and security analysis.
questions.commonMistake: Not enabling Flow Logs and having no visibility into network traffic during security incidents.
questions.followUp: What traffic is NOT captured by Flow Logs?

questions.question: Explain Transit Gateway.
questions.shortAnswer: Hub-and-spoke network transit hub connecting VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect. Simplifies network topology from N*(N-1)/2 peering connections to N connections.
questions.commonMistake: Using VPC peering for 10+ VPCs instead of Transit Gateway — peering becomes unmanageable at scale.
questions.followUp: How does Transit Gateway route table work?

questions.question: What is AWS Direct Connect?
questions.shortAnswer: Dedicated private network connection from on-premises to AWS. 1/10/100 Gbps. Lower latency and more consistent than VPN. Uses BGP for routing.
questions.commonMistake: Not setting up VPN as backup for Direct Connect — DX is not redundant by default.
questions.followUp: How do you achieve high availability with Direct Connect?

questions.question: Design a multi-account VPC architecture for an enterprise.
questions.shortAnswer: Hub-and-spoke with Transit Gateway. Shared services VPC (DNS, monitoring). Network Firewall for inspection. RAM to share TGW across accounts. Centralized egress through firewall VPC.
questions.commonMistake: Creating a full mesh of VPC peering connections — does not scale.
questions.followUp: How do you implement centralized internet egress?

questions.question: How does PrivateLink work?
questions.shortAnswer: Expose services privately across VPCs without VPC peering. Service provider creates NLB + VPC Endpoint Service. Consumer creates Interface VPC Endpoint. Traffic stays on AWS network.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing PrivateLink with VPC peering — PrivateLink is unidirectional and service-specific.
questions.followUp: When would you use PrivateLink vs VPC peering?

questions.question: What is AWS Network Firewall?
questions.shortAnswer: Managed stateful firewall for VPC. Supports IDS/IPS, domain filtering, protocol detection. Deployed in firewall subnet. Routes traffic through firewall endpoints.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying Network Firewall without updating route tables — traffic must be routed through firewall endpoints.
questions.followUp: Network Firewall vs Security Groups vs NACLs vs WAF?

questions.question: Explain IPv6 in VPC.
questions.shortAnswer: VPCs support dual-stack (IPv4 + IPv6). IPv6 CIDRs are public by default (no NAT needed). Use egress-only IGW for outbound IPv6 from private subnets. Security groups and NACLs apply to both.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming IPv6 addresses in VPC are private — they are globally unique and publicly routable.
questions.followUp: What is an Egress-Only Internet Gateway?

questions.question: How do you implement network segmentation?
questions.shortAnswer: Subnets for tier separation (web, app, DB), NACLs for subnet isolation, security groups for instance firewall, VPC peering/TGW for VPC communication, Network Firewall for inspection.
questions.commonMistake: Relying only on security groups without NACLs — defense in depth requires both.
questions.followUp: How do you enforce network segmentation in a multi-account setup?

questions.question: Design a VPC for a 3-tier web application with DR.
questions.shortAnswer: Primary region: VPC with public (ALB), private (app), data (RDS) subnets across 3 AZs. DR region: standby VPC with RDS read replica, S3 CRR, Route 53 failover. VPC peering between regions.
questions.commonMistake: Not separating database subnets from application subnets with dedicated NACLs.
questions.followUp: How do you automate DR failover?

questions.question: Private subnet instances cannot reach the internet. Troubleshoot.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: NAT Gateway exists in public subnet, NAT GW route table has IGW route, private subnet route table has 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT GW, NAT GW security (no SG needed), NAT GW state is "available".
questions.commonMistake: Checking private subnet route table but not verifying the NAT Gateway's own subnet has IGW access.
questions.followUp: How do you troubleshoot NAT Gateway connectivity issues?

questions.question: VPC peering established but instances cannot communicate. Fix it.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: route tables on BOTH sides updated with peer VPC CIDR → pcx-xxx, security groups allow traffic from peer VPC CIDR, NACLs allow traffic, DNS resolution enabled for peering.
questions.commonMistake: Updating route table on only one side. Both VPCs must have routes to each other.
questions.followUp: How do you enable DNS resolution across VPC peering?

questions.question: Migrate from VPC peering to Transit Gateway for 15 VPCs.
questions.shortAnswer: Create TGW, attach VPCs one at a time, update route tables to point to TGW, test connectivity, then remove peering connections. Do it incrementally, not all at once.
questions.commonMistake: Removing peering connections before TGW routes are fully tested — causes downtime.
questions.followUp: How do TGW route tables enable network segmentation?

questions.question: Design network connectivity for hybrid cloud with on-premises data center.
questions.shortAnswer: Primary: Direct Connect for consistent low-latency connectivity. Backup: Site-to-Site VPN over internet. Transit Gateway to connect multiple VPCs. Private VIF for VPC access, Public VIF for public AWS services.
questions.commonMistake: Using only VPN without Direct Connect for latency-sensitive workloads like database replication.
questions.followUp: How do you implement failover from Direct Connect to VPN?

questions.question: Security group rule changes not taking effect.
questions.shortAnswer: SG changes are immediate. Check: correct SG attached to instance, rule direction (inbound vs outbound), protocol and port match, source/destination CIDR correct, instance running latest SG version (no restart needed).
questions.commonMistake: Adding inbound rule on port 80 but the application listens on port 8080.
questions.followUp: How do you audit security group rules across all instances?

questions.question: VPC endpoint not working — requests still going over internet.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: endpoint route in route table (Gateway), DNS resolution (Interface), security group on interface endpoint, endpoint policy allows the action, correct service name used.
questions.commonMistake: For Gateway endpoints: not adding the prefix list route to the route table. For Interface: not using the endpoint DNS name.
questions.followUp: How do you verify traffic is going through the VPC endpoint?

questions.question: Instances in same VPC but different subnets cannot communicate.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: NACLs on both subnets (inbound AND outbound rules including ephemeral ports), security groups allow traffic from other subnet CIDR, route tables have local route for VPC CIDR.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting NACL outbound rules or ephemeral port range (1024-65535) for return traffic.
questions.followUp: What is the default NACL behavior?

questions.question: NAT Gateway data processing charges are very high.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: VPC Flow Logs for traffic patterns, move traffic to VPC endpoints (S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints are free), use S3 gateway endpoint instead of routing S3 traffic through NAT.
questions.commonMistake: Routing S3/DynamoDB traffic through NAT Gateway instead of free Gateway VPC endpoints.
questions.followUp: How do you identify top NAT Gateway traffic sources?

questions.question: Direct Connect link is up but traffic is not flowing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: BGP session state (verify routes being advertised), virtual interface (VIF) state, route table has routes via VGW/DXGW, security groups/NACLs allow traffic, correct VLAN tag.
questions.commonMistake: Not checking BGP route propagation — DX link can be up but BGP may not be advertising routes.
questions.followUp: How do you monitor Direct Connect BGP sessions?

content.html:
Remove Lab Resources

  1. Terminate instances: Delete all EC2 instances in the VPC
  2. Delete NAT Gateway: VPC → NAT Gateways → Delete (wait for deletion)
  3. Release Elastic IP: VPC → Elastic IPs → Release
  4. Delete subnets: VPC → Subnets → Delete all 4
  5. Detach and delete IGW: VPC → Internet Gateways → Detach → Delete
  6. Delete VPC: VPC → Your VPCs → Delete
⚠️
Delete in Order
Delete instances first, then NAT GW, then subnets, then IGW, then VPC. Dependencies must be removed first.

title: Amazon CloudWatch — Monitor Everything
description: Metrics, alarms, Logs, Logs Insights, dashboards, custom metrics, and EMF.
subtitle: Amazon CloudWatch — Monitoring & Observability
objectives: Navigate CloudWatch metrics and understand namespaces, dimensions, and statistics
Create CloudWatch Alarms with SNS notifications for production alerting
Publish custom metrics from Lambda and EC2 applications
Query CloudWatch Logs Insights for operational debugging
Build operational dashboards with widgets for key metrics
Use Metric Filters to extract metrics from log patterns
Implement composite alarms for complex alerting logic

content.html:
📊
You Can't Fix What You Can't See
CloudWatch is the central nervous system of AWS. Every service emits metrics and logs to CloudWatch automatically. Without monitoring, you're flying blind — outages, performance degradation, and cost overruns go undetected until customers complain.
ComponentPurposeExample
MetricsTime-series numerical dataCPUUtilization, Invocations, 4XXError
AlarmsWatch metrics and trigger actionsCPU > 80% for 5 min → notify SNS
LogsCentralized log collectionLambda execution logs, VPC Flow Logs
Logs InsightsSQL-like log queriesFind all ERROR logs in last 1 hour
DashboardsVisual operational displaysReal-time application health view
Events/EventBridgeReact to state changesEC2 instance stopped → notify team
💡
Free Tier: 10 Custom Metrics, 5 GB Log Data, 3 Dashboards
CloudWatch free tier is generous for small workloads. But custom metrics ($0.30/metric/month) and Log data ingestion ($0.50/GB) add up quickly at scale. Use Embedded Metric Format (EMF) for cost-efficient custom metrics.

nodes.label: Lambda
nodes.description: Lambda auto-publishes: Invocations, Duration, Errors, Throttles, ConcurrentExecutions. Logs go to /aws/lambda/<fn-name>.

nodes.label: EC2
nodes.description: EC2 auto-publishes: CPUUtilization, NetworkIn/Out, DiskReadOps. Install CloudWatch Agent for memory, disk, custom metrics.

nodes.label: CloudWatch Metrics
nodes.description: Time-series data organized by Namespace (AWS/Lambda), MetricName, Dimensions (FunctionName). Stored for 15 months at decreasing resolution.

nodes.label: CloudWatch Logs
nodes.description: Log Groups → Log Streams. Retention: configurable (1 day to 10 years or never expire). Query with Logs Insights.

nodes.label: Alarm
nodes.description: Monitors a metric against a threshold. States: OK, ALARM, INSUFFICIENT_DATA. Actions: SNS, Auto Scaling, EC2 action.

nodes.label: Dashboard

nodes.label: Logs Insights

content.html:
1. Metric Anatomy

Namespace:  AWS/Lambda
MetricName: Duration
Dimensions: FunctionName=MyFunc, Resource=MyFunc:$LATEST
Statistics: Average, Sum, Min, Max, p99
Period:     60 seconds (1-minute resolution)

2. Alarm Configuration

  • Threshold: Static value or anomaly detection band
  • Evaluation Periods: "3 out of 5 data points breaching" = reduces noise
  • Actions: SNS topic, Auto Scaling policy, EC2 stop/terminate
  • Composite Alarm: AND/OR logic across multiple alarms (e.g., CPU high AND memory high)

3. Logs Insights Query Language

# Find coldest Lambda cold starts
fields @timestamp, @duration, @billedDuration
| filter @type = "REPORT"
| filter @initDuration > 0
| sort @initDuration desc
| limit 20

# Count errors per function in last 1 hour
fields @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count(*) as errorCount by @logStream
| sort errorCount desc

4. Custom Metrics

Two methods:

  • PutMetricData API: Explicitly publish metrics. $0.30/metric/month.
  • Embedded Metric Format (EMF): Print structured JSON to stdout. CloudWatch extracts metrics automatically. Same cost but easier in Lambda.

5. Metric Resolution

ResolutionRetention
1-second (high-res)3 hours
60-second15 days
5-minute63 days
1-hour455 days (15 months)

content.title: Custom Metrics, Alarms & Log Queries

languages.label: Custom Metrics & Alarms
languages.code:
import boto3
import json
import logging
from datetime import datetime

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

cw = boto3.client('cloudwatch')

def publish_custom_metric(metric_name, value, unit, dimensions):
    """Publish a custom CloudWatch metric."""
    cw.put_metric_data(
        Namespace='MyApp/Orders',
        MetricData=[{
            'MetricName': metric_name,
            'Value': value,
            'Unit': unit,                # Count, Seconds, Bytes, etc.
            'Timestamp': datetime.utcnow(),
            'Dimensions': [
                {'Name': k, 'Value': v}
                for k, v in dimensions.items()
            ]
        }]
    )
    logger.info("Published metric: %s = %s %s", metric_name, value, unit)


def create_alarm(alarm_name, metric_name, threshold, sns_arn):
    """Create a CloudWatch alarm."""
    cw.put_metric_alarm(
        AlarmName=alarm_name,
        Namespace='MyApp/Orders',
        MetricName=metric_name,
        Statistic='Sum',
        Period=300,                       # 5 minutes
        EvaluationPeriods=3,             # Must breach 3 of 3 periods
        DatapointsToAlarm=3,
        Threshold=threshold,
        ComparisonOperator='GreaterThanThreshold',
        AlarmActions=[sns_arn],          # Notify on ALARM
        OKActions=[sns_arn],             # Notify on recovery
        TreatMissingData='notBreaching', # Missing data = OK (safe default)
        Tags=[{'Key': 'Team', 'Value': 'Platform'}]
    )
    logger.info("Created alarm: %s (threshold: %s)", alarm_name, threshold)


# EMF — Embedded Metric Format (print to stdout, CW extracts metrics)
def log_emf_metric(order_id, processing_time_ms, order_value):
    """
    Embedded Metric Format: print structured JSON → CloudWatch
    extracts metrics automatically. No PutMetricData API call needed.
    """
    emf = {
        "_aws": {
            "Timestamp": int(datetime.utcnow().timestamp() * 1000),
            "CloudWatchMetrics": [{
                "Namespace": "MyApp/Orders",
                "Dimensions": [["Environment", "Region"]],
                "Metrics": [
                    {"Name": "ProcessingTime", "Unit": "Milliseconds"},
                    {"Name": "OrderValue", "Unit": "None"}
                ]
            }]
        },
        "Environment": "production",
        "Region": "us-east-1",
        "ProcessingTime": processing_time_ms,
        "OrderValue": order_value,
        "orderId": order_id  # Non-metric field — just logged
    }
    print(json.dumps(emf))  # CloudWatch extracts metrics from stdout

explanations.text: put_metric_data publishes to a custom Namespace. Dimensions are key-value pairs that identify the metric source (e.g., Environment=prod).
EvaluationPeriods=3 with DatapointsToAlarm=3 means ALL 3 periods must breach. Use "2 of 3" for critical alarms to reduce noise.
TreatMissingData=notBreaching means "no data = OK." Use "breaching" if missing data itself indicates a problem.
Embedded Metric Format: print JSON with _aws metadata to stdout. CloudWatch Logs automatically extracts metrics — no API calls, lower latency, same cost.

Created alarm: HighOrderErrors (threshold: 10)

content.initialText:
CloudWatch CLI Lab. Try:

items.title: Lambda metrics not appearing
items.error: No metrics visible for a Lambda function in CloudWatch
items.cause: Lambda was never invoked (no data points to publish). Or you're looking in the wrong region. Metrics appear after the first invocation.
items.fix: Invoke the function at least once. Verify you're in the correct region. Metrics may take 1-2 minutes to appear after invocation.

items.title: Alarm stuck in INSUFFICIENT_DATA
items.cause: No metric data points match the specified dimensions, or the period is longer than the data retention for that resolution.
items.fix: Verify the metric exists (list-metrics). Check dimensions match exactly (case-sensitive). Set TreatMissingData=notBreaching if gaps are expected.

items.title: CloudWatch Logs costs too high
items.cause: Log retention set to "Never Expire" (default). High-volume functions logging at DEBUG level. No log filtering.
items.fix: Set retention policies (30 days for dev, 90 days for prod). Lower Lambda log level to INFO/WARN. Use Log Subscription Filters to send specific patterns to cheaper storage (S3/Kinesis Firehose).

items.title: Custom metric not showing in console
items.error: put_metric_data succeeds but metric not visible
items.cause: Custom metrics take 2-5 minutes to appear. Or the Namespace spelling doesn't match what you're searching for (case-sensitive).
items.fix: Wait 5 minutes. Verify the exact Namespace string. Use list-metrics to confirm: aws cloudwatch list-metrics --namespace "MyApp/Orders"

questions.question: You set a CloudWatch Alarm with EvaluationPeriods=5, DatapointsToAlarm=3, Period=60. When does the alarm trigger?

options.text: When the threshold is breached for 5 consecutive minutes
When 3 out of 5 consecutive 1-minute data points breach the threshold
When the metric breaches for 3 seconds
When the average of 5 periods exceeds the threshold

questions.explanation: 3 out of 5 means: within any 5 consecutive 1-minute evaluation periods, if 3 or more data points breach the threshold, the alarm transitions to ALARM state. This "M out of N" pattern reduces false positives from momentary spikes.

questions.question: EC2 reports CPUUtilization automatically. But you need memory utilization. How do you get it?

options.text: Enable detailed monitoring — it includes memory metrics
Install the CloudWatch Agent on the instance to collect and publish memory metrics
Memory utilization is not available in AWS
Use EC2 Systems Manager to automatically publish memory metrics

questions.explanation: EC2 hypervisor can only see CPU, network, and disk I/O from outside the instance. Memory and disk space require an agent INSIDE the OS. Install the CloudWatch Agent (unified agent) to collect memory, disk, and custom app metrics.

questions.question: What is the advantage of Embedded Metric Format (EMF) over PutMetricData for Lambda custom metrics?

options.text: EMF is cheaper — no per-metric cost
EMF avoids an API call (prints to stdout) so it has lower latency and doesn't increase Lambda duration
EMF supports more metric types than PutMetricData
EMF bypasses IAM permissions

questions.explanation: EMF writes structured JSON to stdout. CloudWatch Logs agent extracts metrics asynchronously. No additional API call during Lambda execution = lower latency and no added duration. PutMetricData is an API call that adds ~50-100ms to execution time. Cost is the same for both.

questions.question: What is Amazon CloudWatch and what problem does it solve?
questions.shortAnswer: Amazon CloudWatch is a managed AWS service that monitors AWS resources and applications with metrics, logs, alarms, and dashboards. It eliminates the need to build custom monitoring infrastructure.
questions.commonMistake: Not enabling detailed monitoring (1-minute intervals) for production EC2 instances.
questions.followUp: When would you NOT use Amazon CloudWatch?

questions.question: What are the key components of Amazon CloudWatch?
questions.shortAnswer: Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, Logs, Log Insights, Events/EventBridge, Synthetics, ServiceLens.
questions.commonMistake: Skipping IAM permissions configuration and using overly permissive policies.
questions.followUp: How does Amazon CloudWatch integrate with other AWS services?

questions.question: How is Amazon CloudWatch priced?
questions.shortAnswer: Priced based on usage — requests, data transfer, and provisioned capacity. Free tier available for 12 months.
questions.commonMistake: Not accounting for data transfer costs between services and regions.
questions.followUp: How do you estimate Amazon CloudWatch costs before deployment?

questions.question: What are the security best practices for Amazon CloudWatch?
questions.shortAnswer: Use least-privilege IAM policies, enable encryption at rest and in transit, use VPC endpoints where available, enable CloudTrail logging, and implement resource-based policies.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS managed policies that grant broader access than needed.
questions.followUp: How do you monitor Amazon CloudWatch for security events?

questions.question: How do you monitor Amazon CloudWatch?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudWatch metrics for operational monitoring, CloudWatch Logs for detailed logging, CloudTrail for API auditing, and set up alarms for critical thresholds.
questions.commonMistake: Not setting up alarms for error rates and latency — relying only on dashboards.
questions.followUp: What CloudWatch metrics are most important to monitor?

questions.question: How does Amazon CloudWatch achieve high availability?
questions.shortAnswer: CloudWatch is a regional service that stores data redundantly across AZs. Multi-region dashboards aggregate cross-region data.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying in single AZ for cost savings without understanding availability impact.
questions.followUp: What is the RPO and RTO for Amazon CloudWatch?

questions.question: Explain the Amazon CloudWatch scaling strategy.
questions.shortAnswer: Supports both vertical (instance size) and horizontal (instance count) scaling. Auto-scaling available based on CloudWatch metrics.
questions.commonMistake: Not load testing before production to determine correct scaling thresholds.
questions.followUp: How do you handle scaling during unexpected traffic spikes?

questions.question: How does Amazon CloudWatch handle encryption?
questions.shortAnswer: Supports encryption at rest (KMS keys) and in transit (TLS). Can use AWS-managed or customer-managed KMS keys. Key rotation supported.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS-managed keys when compliance requires customer-managed keys with custom key policies.
questions.followUp: How do you rotate encryption keys without downtime?

questions.question: What are the limits and quotas for Amazon CloudWatch?
questions.shortAnswer: Default: 5000 alarms, 500 metrics per dashboard, 10 custom namespaces. PutMetricData: 150 TPS.
questions.commonMistake: Hitting service limits during peak traffic without having requested increases in advance.
questions.followUp: How do you proactively monitor service quota usage?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon CloudWatch in a multi-account strategy?
questions.shortAnswer: Use AWS Organizations with SCPs, resource sharing via RAM where supported, cross-account IAM roles, and centralized logging.
questions.commonMistake: Not using separate accounts for production and development workloads.
questions.followUp: How do you share resources across accounts securely?

questions.question: Design a production-grade Amazon CloudWatch architecture.
questions.shortAnswer: Multi-AZ deployment, encryption, monitoring with alarms, automated backups, infrastructure as code (CloudFormation/Terraform), blue/green deployments, and disaster recovery plan.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying to production without a runbook for common failure scenarios.
questions.followUp: How do you test disaster recovery for this architecture?

questions.question: How do you optimize Amazon CloudWatch costs?
questions.shortAnswer: Right-size resources using CloudWatch metrics, use Reserved capacity for predictable workloads, implement auto-scaling, clean up unused resources, use Cost Explorer for analysis.
questions.commonMistake: Over-provisioning resources based on peak capacity estimates without actual usage data.
questions.followUp: How do you implement continuous cost optimization?

questions.question: What is the disaster recovery strategy for Amazon CloudWatch?
questions.shortAnswer: Pilot Light: core infrastructure in DR region. Warm Standby: scaled-down version running in DR region. Multi-Site: active-active across regions.
questions.commonMistake: Not regularly testing DR procedures — failover should be rehearsed quarterly.
questions.followUp: How do you automate DR failover?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon CloudWatch using Infrastructure as Code?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudFormation or Terraform to define resources declaratively. Include all dependencies (IAM roles, security groups, monitoring). Use parameters for environment-specific values.
questions.commonMistake: Not parameterizing templates — hardcoding account IDs, region, and environment-specific values.
questions.followUp: How do you handle state management in IaC for this service?

questions.question: What compliance frameworks does Amazon CloudWatch support?
questions.shortAnswer: SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FedRAMP. Use Config rules and Security Hub for continuous compliance monitoring.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming AWS compliance covers your application — shared responsibility model means you must secure your configuration.
questions.followUp: How do you generate compliance evidence for auditors?

questions.question: Your Amazon CloudWatch is experiencing intermittent errors. How do you diagnose?
questions.shortAnswer: Check CloudWatch metrics (error rate, latency, throttling), CloudWatch Logs for error details, X-Ray traces for request flow, CloudTrail for API changes, and service health dashboard.
questions.commonMistake: Only checking application logs without looking at AWS service-level metrics and limits.
questions.followUp: How do you set up proactive alerting for this service?

questions.question: Migrate Amazon CloudWatch from one AWS account to another.
questions.shortAnswer: Export configuration, create resources in target account via IaC, migrate data using service-specific tools, update DNS/endpoints, test, then cutover. Use cross-account roles during migration.
questions.commonMistake: Not planning for the DNS cutover — TTL should be lowered well before migration.
questions.followUp: How do you minimize downtime during migration?

questions.question: Amazon CloudWatch costs have doubled unexpectedly. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Cost Explorer → filter by service and usage type, check for unused resources, verify auto-scaling is working (not just scaling up), check for data transfer costs, review recent configuration changes.
questions.commonMistake: Only looking at compute costs and ignoring data transfer between services/regions.
questions.followUp: How do you set up billing alerts for this service?

questions.question: Design a zero-downtime update strategy for Amazon CloudWatch.
questions.shortAnswer: Blue/green deployment: create new version alongside old, test new version, switch traffic gradually (canary → full), rollback instantly if issues. Use CloudFormation update policies.
questions.commonMistake: Not having a rollback plan — every deployment should have a tested rollback procedure.
questions.followUp: How do you implement canary deployments?

questions.question: Your team needs to access Amazon CloudWatch across 5 AWS accounts. Design the access pattern.
questions.shortAnswer: IAM Identity Center with permission sets per account/role. Cross-account roles for programmatic access. Centralized logging account for audit. RAM for resource sharing where applicable.
questions.commonMistake: Creating separate IAM users in each account instead of using centralized SSO.
questions.followUp: How do you enforce least privilege across accounts?

questions.question: Amazon CloudWatch API calls are being throttled.
questions.shortAnswer: Implement exponential backoff with jitter, check service quotas and request increases, cache responses, use batch operations where available, distribute requests across time.
questions.commonMistake: Retrying throttled requests immediately without backoff, making the throttling worse.
questions.followUp: How do you design applications to be resilient to API throttling?

questions.question: Amazon CloudWatch has high latency. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: CloudWatch latency metrics, network connectivity (VPC endpoints vs internet), resource right-sizing, connection pooling, caching layer, regional endpoint proximity.
questions.commonMistake: Not using VPC endpoints — traffic going over internet instead of AWS backbone adds latency.
questions.followUp: How do you implement caching to reduce latency?

questions.question: Cannot access Amazon CloudWatch from Lambda function.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: Lambda execution role has required permissions, Lambda is in VPC with correct subnets/SG, VPC endpoint exists or NAT Gateway for internet access, resource-based policy allows Lambda.
questions.commonMistake: Putting Lambda in VPC without NAT Gateway or VPC endpoint — Lambda loses internet access.
questions.followUp: When should you put Lambda in a VPC vs outside VPC?

questions.question: Amazon CloudWatch encryption at rest is failing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: KMS key policy allows the service principal, key is in the same region, key is not disabled/pending deletion, IAM role has kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt permissions.
questions.commonMistake: Using a KMS key from a different region — KMS keys are regional.
questions.followUp: How do you troubleshoot KMS key policy issues?

questions.question: CloudWatch metrics for Amazon CloudWatch are missing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: detailed monitoring enabled (not just basic), correct namespace and metric name, data exists for the time range, metric dimensions correct, IAM permissions for CloudWatch.
questions.commonMistake: Looking at the wrong CloudWatch namespace or not enabling detailed monitoring.
questions.followUp: How do you create custom metrics for this service?

intro: Master AWS observability. Covers metrics, custom metrics, alarms, Log Groups/Streams, Metric Filters, Logs Insights queries, dashboards, and anomaly detection.

title: Amazon RDS — Relational Databases
description: Managed databases: Multi-AZ, Read Replicas, Aurora, RDS Proxy, backups, and Lambda integration.
subtitle: Amazon RDS — Relational Database Service
objectives: Choose the right RDS engine for your workload (Aurora vs standard)
Configure Multi-AZ for high availability with automatic failover
Implement Read Replicas for read-heavy workloads
Manage automated backups, snapshots, and point-in-time recovery
Connect Lambda to RDS using RDS Proxy for connection pooling
Secure RDS with encryption, VPC isolation, and IAM authentication
Monitor RDS performance with Enhanced Monitoring and Performance Insights

content.html:
🗄️
Managed Databases — Don't Be a DBA
RDS automates the undifferentiated heavy lifting: patching, backups, failover, scaling, and replication. You get a production-grade database in minutes instead of weeks. Focus on your schema and queries, not on managing database servers.

Engine Comparison

EnginePerformanceStorageCostBest For
Aurora MySQL5x MySQL perfUp to 128 TB, auto-grows~20% more than RDS MySQLProduction apps needing MySQL compatibility + scale
Aurora PostgreSQL3x PostgreSQL perfUp to 128 TB, auto-grows~20% more than RDS PostgreSQLComplex queries, GIS, full-text search
RDS MySQLStandardUp to 64 TBLowerSimple web apps, WordPress
RDS PostgreSQLStandardUp to 64 TBLowerWhen 100% PostgreSQL compatibility needed
Aurora Serverless v2Scales automaticallyUp to 128 TBPay per ACU-secondVariable/unpredictable workloads
⚠️
Lambda + RDS = Connection Exhaustion Risk
Each Lambda invocation opens a new database connection. With 1000 concurrent Lambdas, you'll exhaust the RDS connection limit (typically 150-3000). Always use RDS Proxy between Lambda and RDS for connection pooling.

content.title: Multi-AZ RDS with Read Replicas & RDS Proxy

nodes.label: Application / Lambda
nodes.description: Application writes and reads to the database. Lambda should always connect through RDS Proxy.

nodes.label: RDS Proxy
nodes.description: Connection pooler for RDS. Maintains a warm pool of connections. Multiplexes many Lambda connections through few DB connections. Handles failover transparently.

nodes.label: Primary (AZ-a)
nodes.description: Primary RDS instance handles all writes and reads. Synchronously replicates to standby for Multi-AZ.

nodes.label: Standby (AZ-b)
nodes.description: Multi-AZ standby receives synchronous replication. Not readable. Automatic failover in ~60 seconds if primary fails. DNS endpoint stays the same.

nodes.label: Read Replica
nodes.description: Asynchronous replication from primary. Readable. Use for read-heavy queries, reports, analytics. Can be cross-region for DR. Can be promoted to standalone.

nodes.label: Automated Backup
nodes.description: Daily automated snapshots + transaction logs. Point-in-time recovery to any second in the retention period (up to 35 days). Stored in S3 (managed by AWS).

content.html:
1. Multi-AZ vs Read Replicas

FeatureMulti-AZRead Replica
PurposeHigh availability (failover)Read scalability
ReplicationSynchronousAsynchronous
Readable?No (standby only)Yes — serves read queries
FailoverAutomatic (~60s), same DNSManual promotion
Cross-RegionNo (same region only)Yes — cross-region supported
Cost2x (standby instance)Per replica instance

2. RDS Proxy (Critical for Lambda)

RDS Proxy sits between your application and the database:

  • Maintains a pool of warm connections to RDS
  • Multiplexes thousands of Lambda connections through a small pool
  • Handles failover transparently — no connection string changes
  • Supports IAM authentication — no passwords in code

3. Backup & Recovery

  • Automated Backups: Daily snapshots + continuous transaction log backup. Retention: 0-35 days. Point-in-time recovery to any second.
  • Manual Snapshots: User-initiated. Persist until explicitly deleted. Share cross-account or cross-region.
  • Restore: Restores create a NEW RDS instance — you cannot restore in-place.

4. Encryption

  • At rest: KMS encryption of storage, snapshots, replicas, and logs. Must be enabled at creation — cannot encrypt an existing unencrypted DB.
  • In transit: SSL/TLS. Force with rds.force_ssl=1 parameter.

5. Parameter Groups & Option Groups

  • DB Parameter Group: Database engine configuration (max_connections, query_cache_size, log_slow_queries). Like my.cnf for MySQL.
  • DB Option Group: Engine-specific features (Oracle APEX, MySQL memcached plugin).

6. Aurora Serverless v2

Scales in ACU (Aurora Capacity Units) increments of 0.5. Scales from 0.5 ACU to 128 ACU in seconds. Pay only for capacity used. Ideal for dev/test (scale to near-zero) and variable production workloads.

content.title: Connect Lambda to RDS via RDS Proxy

languages.label: Lambda + RDS Proxy
languages.code:
import boto3
import json
import os
import logging
import pymysql

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

# RDS Proxy endpoint — NOT the direct RDS endpoint
PROXY_ENDPOINT = os.environ['RDS_PROXY_ENDPOINT']
DB_NAME = os.environ['DB_NAME']
DB_USER = os.environ['DB_USER']
REGION  = os.environ.get('AWS_REGION', 'us-east-1')

# Global connection — reuse across warm invocations
connection = None

def get_connection():
    """
    Get or reuse a database connection.
    Uses IAM authentication — no passwords in code or env vars.
    """
    global connection
    if connection and connection.open:
        return connection

    # Generate IAM auth token (temporary password, 15-min validity)
    rds_client = boto3.client('rds')
    token = rds_client.generate_db_auth_token(
        DBHostname=PROXY_ENDPOINT,
        Port=3306,
        DBUsername=DB_USER,
        Region=REGION
    )

    connection = pymysql.connect(
        host=PROXY_ENDPOINT,
        user=DB_USER,
        password=token,           # IAM auth token as password
        database=DB_NAME,
        port=3306,
        connect_timeout=5,
        ssl={'ca': '/opt/rds-combined-ca-bundle.pem'},  # SSL required
        cursorclass=pymysql.cursors.DictCursor
    )
    logger.info("Connected to RDS via Proxy: %s", PROXY_ENDPOINT)
    return connection


def lambda_handler(event, context):
    """Query RDS through RDS Proxy with connection reuse."""
    conn = get_connection()

    try:
        with conn.cursor() as cursor:
            cursor.execute(
                "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = %s ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10",
                (event.get('userId'),)
            )
            orders = cursor.fetchall()

        return {
            'statusCode': 200,
            'body': json.dumps(orders, default=str)
        }

    except pymysql.err.OperationalError as e:
        logger.error("Database error: %s", str(e))
        # Reset connection on error — next invocation will reconnect
        connection = None
        return {
            'statusCode': 500,
            'body': json.dumps({'error': 'Database connection error'})
        }

explanations.text: CRITICAL: Use the RDS Proxy endpoint, not the direct RDS endpoint. Proxy handles connection pooling and failover.
Global connection variable — reused across warm Lambda invocations (same execution environment). Saves ~100ms connection setup time.
IAM authentication: generate_db_auth_token creates a temporary password (15 min). No static passwords. Requires IAM policy with rds-db:connect.

items.title: Lambda "Too many connections" error
items.cause: Each Lambda invocation opens a new connection. 1000 concurrent Lambdas = 1000 connections. RDS max_connections is typically 150-3000 depending on instance class.
items.fix: Use RDS Proxy (connection pooling). Set reserved concurrency on Lambda to limit max connections. Reuse connections across warm invocations (global variable).

items.title: RDS Multi-AZ failover causing errors
items.error: Application errors during maintenance window or AZ failure
items.cause: Multi-AZ failover takes ~60 seconds. During failover, DNS switches to the standby but cached DNS entries point to the old primary.
items.fix: Use RDS Proxy (handles failover transparently). Set DNS TTL to 30 seconds in your application. Implement connection retry logic with exponential backoff.

items.title: Read Replica lag increasing
items.error: Read Replica shows increasing replication lag (seconds behind primary)
items.cause: Write-heavy workload on primary exceeds replica's apply capacity. Long-running queries on replica block replication.
items.fix: Scale up the replica instance class. Use Aurora (parallel replication). Avoid long-running queries on replicas. Monitor ReplicaLag CloudWatch metric.

items.title: Cannot connect to RDS from Lambda
items.error: Lambda times out when connecting to RDS
items.cause: Lambda is in a VPC but the Security Group or subnet configuration doesn't allow outbound access to the RDS port (3306/5432).
items.fix: Verify: 1) Lambda SG allows outbound on port 3306/5432. 2) RDS SG allows inbound from Lambda SG. 3) Lambda is in a subnet that can reach RDS (same VPC). 4) Lambda has VPC config with correct subnets and SGs.

questions.explanation: Multi-AZ is automatic failover. AWS detects the failure, updates the DNS CNAME to point to the standby, and the standby becomes the new primary. ~60 seconds downtime. No manual intervention needed. The database endpoint URL does not change.

questions.explanation: Lambda scales to thousands of concurrent invocations. Each opens a database connection. RDS typically supports 150-3000 max connections. RDS Proxy maintains a warm connection pool and multiplexes many Lambda connections through few DB connections, preventing "Too many connections" errors.

questions.question: You need disaster recovery for an Aurora database across regions. What approach should you use?

Aurora Global Database — provides cross-region replication with <1 second lag and fast cross-region failover
Manually copy snapshots to another region daily
Use DynamoDB Global Tables instead

questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database replicates an entire Aurora cluster to up to 5 secondary regions with typically <1 second replication lag. Cross-region failover promotes a secondary region in under 1 minute. Multi-AZ only works within a single region.

questions.question: What is Amazon RDS and what problem does it solve?
questions.shortAnswer: Amazon RDS is a managed AWS service that provides managed relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Aurora). It eliminates the need to manage database servers, patching, backups, and high availability.
questions.commonMistake: Not enabling Multi-AZ for production databases.
questions.followUp: When would you NOT use Amazon RDS?

questions.question: What are the key components of Amazon RDS?
questions.shortAnswer: DB Instance, DB Subnet Group, Parameter Group, Option Group, Snapshots, Read Replicas, Multi-AZ.
questions.commonMistake: Skipping IAM permissions configuration and using overly permissive policies.
questions.followUp: How does Amazon RDS integrate with other AWS services?

questions.question: How is Amazon RDS priced?
questions.shortAnswer: Priced based on usage — requests, data transfer, and provisioned capacity. Free tier available for 12 months.
questions.commonMistake: Not accounting for data transfer costs between services and regions.
questions.followUp: How do you estimate Amazon RDS costs before deployment?

questions.question: What are the security best practices for Amazon RDS?
questions.shortAnswer: Use least-privilege IAM policies, enable encryption at rest and in transit, use VPC endpoints where available, enable CloudTrail logging, and implement resource-based policies.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS managed policies that grant broader access than needed.
questions.followUp: How do you monitor Amazon RDS for security events?

questions.question: How do you monitor Amazon RDS?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudWatch metrics for operational monitoring, CloudWatch Logs for detailed logging, CloudTrail for API auditing, and set up alarms for critical thresholds.
questions.commonMistake: Not setting up alarms for error rates and latency — relying only on dashboards.
questions.followUp: What CloudWatch metrics are most important to monitor?

questions.question: How does Amazon RDS achieve high availability?
questions.shortAnswer: Multi-AZ: synchronous replication to standby in different AZ. Automatic failover in ~60 seconds. Aurora: 6 copies across 3 AZs.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying in single AZ for cost savings without understanding availability impact.
questions.followUp: What is the RPO and RTO for Amazon RDS?

questions.question: Explain the Amazon RDS scaling strategy.
questions.shortAnswer: Vertical: change instance class (brief downtime). Horizontal reads: up to 15 read replicas. Aurora auto-scaling read replicas.
questions.commonMistake: Not load testing before production to determine correct scaling thresholds.
questions.followUp: How do you handle scaling during unexpected traffic spikes?

questions.question: How does Amazon RDS handle encryption?
questions.shortAnswer: Supports encryption at rest (KMS keys) and in transit (TLS). Can use AWS-managed or customer-managed KMS keys. Key rotation supported.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS-managed keys when compliance requires customer-managed keys with custom key policies.
questions.followUp: How do you rotate encryption keys without downtime?

questions.question: What are the limits and quotas for Amazon RDS?
questions.shortAnswer: Default: 40 DB instances per region, max storage 64 TB (Aurora: 128 TB), 5 read replicas (Aurora: 15).
questions.commonMistake: Hitting service limits during peak traffic without having requested increases in advance.
questions.followUp: How do you proactively monitor service quota usage?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon RDS in a multi-account strategy?
questions.shortAnswer: Use AWS Organizations with SCPs, resource sharing via RAM where supported, cross-account IAM roles, and centralized logging.
questions.commonMistake: Not using separate accounts for production and development workloads.
questions.followUp: How do you share resources across accounts securely?

questions.question: Design a production-grade Amazon RDS architecture.
questions.shortAnswer: Multi-AZ deployment, encryption, monitoring with alarms, automated backups, infrastructure as code (CloudFormation/Terraform), blue/green deployments, and disaster recovery plan.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying to production without a runbook for common failure scenarios.
questions.followUp: How do you test disaster recovery for this architecture?

questions.question: How do you optimize Amazon RDS costs?
questions.shortAnswer: Right-size resources using CloudWatch metrics, use Reserved capacity for predictable workloads, implement auto-scaling, clean up unused resources, use Cost Explorer for analysis.
questions.commonMistake: Over-provisioning resources based on peak capacity estimates without actual usage data.
questions.followUp: How do you implement continuous cost optimization?

questions.question: What is the disaster recovery strategy for Amazon RDS?
questions.shortAnswer: Pilot Light: core infrastructure in DR region. Warm Standby: scaled-down version running in DR region. Multi-Site: active-active across regions.
questions.commonMistake: Not regularly testing DR procedures — failover should be rehearsed quarterly.
questions.followUp: How do you automate DR failover?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon RDS using Infrastructure as Code?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudFormation or Terraform to define resources declaratively. Include all dependencies (IAM roles, security groups, monitoring). Use parameters for environment-specific values.
questions.commonMistake: Not parameterizing templates — hardcoding account IDs, region, and environment-specific values.
questions.followUp: How do you handle state management in IaC for this service?

questions.question: What compliance frameworks does Amazon RDS support?
questions.shortAnswer: SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FedRAMP. Use Config rules and Security Hub for continuous compliance monitoring.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming AWS compliance covers your application — shared responsibility model means you must secure your configuration.
questions.followUp: How do you generate compliance evidence for auditors?

questions.question: Your Amazon RDS is experiencing intermittent errors. How do you diagnose?
questions.shortAnswer: Check CloudWatch metrics (error rate, latency, throttling), CloudWatch Logs for error details, X-Ray traces for request flow, CloudTrail for API changes, and service health dashboard.
questions.commonMistake: Only checking application logs without looking at AWS service-level metrics and limits.
questions.followUp: How do you set up proactive alerting for this service?

questions.question: Migrate Amazon RDS from one AWS account to another.
questions.shortAnswer: Export configuration, create resources in target account via IaC, migrate data using service-specific tools, update DNS/endpoints, test, then cutover. Use cross-account roles during migration.
questions.commonMistake: Not planning for the DNS cutover — TTL should be lowered well before migration.
questions.followUp: How do you minimize downtime during migration?

questions.question: Amazon RDS costs have doubled unexpectedly. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Cost Explorer → filter by service and usage type, check for unused resources, verify auto-scaling is working (not just scaling up), check for data transfer costs, review recent configuration changes.
questions.commonMistake: Only looking at compute costs and ignoring data transfer between services/regions.
questions.followUp: How do you set up billing alerts for this service?

questions.question: Design a zero-downtime update strategy for Amazon RDS.
questions.shortAnswer: Blue/green deployment: create new version alongside old, test new version, switch traffic gradually (canary → full), rollback instantly if issues. Use CloudFormation update policies.
questions.commonMistake: Not having a rollback plan — every deployment should have a tested rollback procedure.
questions.followUp: How do you implement canary deployments?

questions.question: Your team needs to access Amazon RDS across 5 AWS accounts. Design the access pattern.
questions.shortAnswer: IAM Identity Center with permission sets per account/role. Cross-account roles for programmatic access. Centralized logging account for audit. RAM for resource sharing where applicable.
questions.commonMistake: Creating separate IAM users in each account instead of using centralized SSO.
questions.followUp: How do you enforce least privilege across accounts?

questions.question: Amazon RDS API calls are being throttled.
questions.shortAnswer: Implement exponential backoff with jitter, check service quotas and request increases, cache responses, use batch operations where available, distribute requests across time.
questions.commonMistake: Retrying throttled requests immediately without backoff, making the throttling worse.
questions.followUp: How do you design applications to be resilient to API throttling?

questions.question: Amazon RDS has high latency. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: CloudWatch latency metrics, network connectivity (VPC endpoints vs internet), resource right-sizing, connection pooling, caching layer, regional endpoint proximity.
questions.commonMistake: Not using VPC endpoints — traffic going over internet instead of AWS backbone adds latency.
questions.followUp: How do you implement caching to reduce latency?

questions.question: Cannot access Amazon RDS from Lambda function.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: Lambda execution role has required permissions, Lambda is in VPC with correct subnets/SG, VPC endpoint exists or NAT Gateway for internet access, resource-based policy allows Lambda.
questions.commonMistake: Putting Lambda in VPC without NAT Gateway or VPC endpoint — Lambda loses internet access.
questions.followUp: When should you put Lambda in a VPC vs outside VPC?

questions.question: Amazon RDS encryption at rest is failing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: KMS key policy allows the service principal, key is in the same region, key is not disabled/pending deletion, IAM role has kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt permissions.
questions.commonMistake: Using a KMS key from a different region — KMS keys are regional.
questions.followUp: How do you troubleshoot KMS key policy issues?

questions.question: CloudWatch metrics for Amazon RDS are missing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: detailed monitoring enabled (not just basic), correct namespace and metric name, data exists for the time range, metric dimensions correct, IAM permissions for CloudWatch.
questions.commonMistake: Looking at the wrong CloudWatch namespace or not enabling detailed monitoring.
questions.followUp: How do you create custom metrics for this service?

title: Amazon Route 53 — DNS & Domain Names
description: DNS service: hosted zones, record types, routing policies, health checks, and failover.
subtitle: Amazon Route 53 — DNS & Traffic Management
objectives: Create and manage Route 53 Hosted Zones for domain management
Differentiate between record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, and Alias records
Implement routing policies for load balancing and disaster recovery
Configure health checks for automated failover
Use Alias records to point to AWS resources (ALB, CloudFront, S3)
Register and transfer domains through Route 53
Design multi-region active-active and active-passive architectures

content.html:
🌐
DNS is the Foundation of Every Web Application
Route 53 is a highly available, scalable DNS service with 100% uptime SLA. It translates human-friendly domain names (api.example.com) to IP addresses and AWS resource endpoints. Named after TCP/UDP port 53 — the DNS port.

Record Types

TypePoints ToUse Case
AIPv4 addressMap domain to an IP: 203.0.113.1
AAAAIPv6 addressMap domain to IPv6
CNAMEAnother domain nameRedirect api.example.com → lb-123.elb.amazonaws.com
AliasAWS resource directlyFree, works at zone apex, native AWS integration
MXMail serversEmail routing
TXTText dataDomain verification, SPF, DKIM
NSName serversDelegation (auto-created per hosted zone)
💡
Alias Records > CNAME for AWS Resources
Alias records are free (no query charges), work at the zone apex (example.com, not just sub.example.com), and resolve directly to the resource IP. CNAME adds an extra DNS hop and cannot be used at the zone apex. Always prefer Alias for ALB, CloudFront, S3, and API Gateway.

content.title: Route 53 Failover Routing with Health Checks

nodes.label: User Browser
nodes.description: User types api.example.com in the browser. The browser makes a DNS query to resolve the domain to an IP address.

nodes.label: Route 53
nodes.description: Route 53 receives the DNS query. Evaluates the routing policy and health check status. Returns the appropriate IP/endpoint based on the active routing policy.

nodes.label: Health Checks
nodes.description: Route 53 health checkers ping your endpoints every 10 or 30 seconds from multiple regions. If an endpoint fails, Route 53 stops routing traffic to it.

nodes.label: Primary (us-east-1)
nodes.description: Primary ALB in us-east-1. Active target for failover routing. Health check monitors /health endpoint.

nodes.label: Secondary (eu-west-1)
nodes.description: Secondary ALB in eu-west-1. Standby for failover. Route 53 routes here only if primary health check fails.

nodes.label: CloudFront
nodes.description: For static content, Route 53 Alias record points to CloudFront distribution. Cached at 400+ edge locations globally.

content.html:
1. Hosted Zones

  • Public Hosted Zone: Resolves domains on the public internet. Cost: $0.50/month per zone.
  • Private Hosted Zone: Resolves domains only within associated VPCs. For internal service discovery (db.internal.myapp.com).

2. Routing Policies

PolicyHow It WorksUse Case
SimpleReturns a single value (or random from multiple)Single resource, no health checks
WeightedDistributes traffic by percentage (e.g., 70/30)Blue-green deployments, canary releases
LatencyRoutes to the region with lowest latency for the userMulti-region apps, global user base
FailoverPrimary/secondary — routes to secondary if primary failsDisaster recovery, active-passive HA
GeolocationRoutes based on user's geographic locationContent localization, compliance (data residency)
GeoproximityRoutes based on proximity with bias shiftingFine-tuned geographic routing with bias to shift traffic between regions
Multi-Value AnswerReturns up to 8 healthy records randomlyClient-side load balancing with health checks

3. Health Checks

  • HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP protocol
  • Interval: 10 or 30 seconds (10s costs more)
  • Threshold: number of consecutive checks to mark healthy/unhealthy
  • String matching: check if response body contains a specific string
  • Calculated health checks: AND/OR logic across multiple checks

4. Alias vs CNAME

FeatureAliasCNAME
Zone apex (example.com)?✅ Yes❌ No
DNS query charge?Free for AWS resourcesStandard charges
TargetsALB, CloudFront, S3, API Gateway, etc.Any hostname
Health check integrationInherits from targetMust configure separately

5. TTL (Time to Live)

DNS caching duration in seconds. Lower TTL = faster failover but more DNS queries (more cost). Higher TTL = fewer queries but slower failover. Alias records don't have configurable TTL — Route 53 sets it automatically.

content.title: Manage DNS Records Programmatically

languages.label: DNS Record Management

explanations.text: UPSERT creates the record if it doesn't exist or updates it if it does. Safer than CREATE which fails if the record exists.
SetIdentifier is required for routing policies (failover, weighted, latency, etc.). Must be unique within the record set.
AliasTarget for ALB: HostedZoneId is the ALB's hosted zone (not your hosted zone). Each region has a specific ALB hosted zone ID.
HealthCheckId on PRIMARY record — Route 53 routes to SECONDARY when this health check fails.
FailureThreshold=3 means 3 consecutive failed checks mark the endpoint unhealthy. With RequestInterval=30s, failover triggers in ~90 seconds.

Failover records created: PENDING

  aws route53 list-health-checks

items.title: DNS changes not taking effect
items.error: Updated Route 53 record but domain still resolves to old IP
items.cause: DNS caching at multiple levels: browser, OS resolver, ISP recursive resolver. Old records cached for TTL duration.
items.fix: Wait for the previous TTL to expire (check with dig or nslookup). Lower TTL to 60 seconds BEFORE making changes, wait for old TTL to expire, then make the change. After propagation, raise TTL back.

items.title: CNAME at zone apex fails
items.error: Cannot create CNAME record for example.com (only sub.example.com)
items.cause: DNS RFC prohibits CNAME records at the zone apex because CNAME would conflict with the required SOA and NS records.
items.fix: Use Route 53 Alias record instead of CNAME. Alias records work at the zone apex and are free for AWS resource targets.

items.title: Health check failing unexpectedly
items.error: Route 53 health check reports "Failure" but the endpoint is accessible
items.cause: Route 53 health checkers come from AWS IP ranges. If your Security Group or firewall doesn't allow these IPs, health checks fail.
items.fix: Allow Route 53 health checker IP ranges in your Security Group/firewall. AWS publishes these at https://ip-ranges.amazonaws.com/ip-ranges.json (filter for service=ROUTE53_HEALTHCHECKS).

items.title: Failover routing not switching to secondary
items.error: Primary endpoint is down but traffic not routing to secondary
items.cause: Health check is checking wrong port/path, or EvaluateTargetHealth not enabled on Alias target, or health check interval + threshold haven't been exceeded yet.
items.fix: Verify health check path matches your app's health endpoint. Set EvaluateTargetHealth=true on Alias target. With RequestInterval=30s and FailureThreshold=3, failover takes ~90 seconds minimum.

questions.question: You want to route api.example.com to an ALB. Should you use a CNAME record or an Alias record?

options.text: CNAME — it supports pointing to other hostnames
Alias — it's free for AWS resources, faster (no extra DNS hop), and works at the zone apex
A record with the ALB's IP address
Either works identically

questions.explanation: Alias records are the correct choice for AWS resources. They're free (no per-query charge), resolve directly to the target IP (no extra DNS hop like CNAME), integrate with health checks natively, and work at the zone apex (example.com). ALB IPs change dynamically, so you cannot use a static A record.

questions.question: You want to do a canary deployment: 10% of traffic to the new version, 90% to the current version. Which routing policy should you use?

options.text: Simple routing with two A records
Failover routing with health checks
Weighted routing with 10/90 weight split
Latency routing across two regions

questions.explanation: Weighted routing distributes traffic by percentage based on weights. Set weight=10 for the canary and weight=90 for the stable version. Gradually increase the canary weight as confidence builds. Add health checks to auto-remove unhealthy endpoints.

questions.question: Your app serves users globally from us-east-1 and eu-west-1. You want each user routed to the region with the lowest latency. Which routing policy do you use?

options.text: Geolocation routing — routes based on user location
Latency-based routing — routes to the region with lowest measured latency
Weighted routing with 50/50 split
Simple routing with both IPs

questions.explanation: Latency-based routing measures the actual network latency between the user and each region, then routes to the fastest. Geolocation routes by country/continent (not latency). A user in London might have lower latency to us-east-1 than eu-west-1 due to network topology — latency routing would correctly route there.
