title: Amazon Cognito — User Authentication
description: User authentication, OAuth 2.0, user pools, identity pools, and Lambda triggers.
subtitle: Amazon Cognito — Authentication & Authorization
objectives: Explain the difference between Cognito User Pools and Identity Pools
Implement user sign-up, sign-in, and token refresh flows
Validate Cognito JWTs in a Lambda function without a library
Configure API Gateway Cognito Authorizer to protect endpoints
Use Lambda triggers to customize authentication flows
Implement MFA and password policies
Map Cognito groups to IAM roles for authorization

content.html:
🔐
Authentication is Hard — Let AWS Handle It
Building secure authentication from scratch requires: secure password hashing, brute-force protection, MFA, token management, refresh flows, PKCE, and compliance (SOC2, HIPAA). Cognito provides all of this as a managed service.
Cognito ComponentPurposeWhat it Issues
User PoolUser directory — sign-up, sign-in, MFA, password policiesJWT tokens: ID token, Access token, Refresh token
Identity PoolFederated identity — exchange tokens for temporary AWS credentialsSTS temporary credentials (AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, SessionToken)

The most common serverless pattern:

  1. User authenticates against Cognito User Pool → receives JWT tokens
  2. Client sends JWT in Authorization: Bearer <token> header
  3. API Gateway Cognito Authorizer validates the JWT automatically
  4. Lambda receives the verified user claims in event.requestContext.authorizer.claims

content.title: Amazon Cognito → API Gateway → Lambda Auth Flow

nodes.label: Mobile/Web App
nodes.description: Client application handles the auth UI and token storage.

nodes.label: Cognito User Pool
nodes.description: User Pool authenticates credentials and issues JWT tokens. Hosts the hosted UI for OAuth2 flows.

nodes.label: API Gateway + Cognito Authorizer
nodes.description: API Gateway Cognito Authorizer validates the JWT signature using the User Pool's public keys (JWKS). No Lambda invocation needed — it's native.

nodes.label: Lambda
nodes.description: Lambda receives pre-validated claims in event.requestContext.authorizer.claims — no JWT validation code needed.

nodes.label: Identity Pool
nodes.description: Identity Pool exchanges User Pool JWT for temporary AWS credentials via STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.

nodes.label: STS
nodes.description: STS issues short-lived credentials (1 hour) mapped to the appropriate IAM role based on Cognito group membership.

content.html:
1. JWT Token Structure

Cognito issues three tokens:

  • ID Token: Contains user attributes (email, name, phone). Use this for identity in your app.
  • Access Token: Used to call Cognito APIs (GetUser, etc.) and to authorize API Gateway calls.
  • Refresh Token: Long-lived (30 days by default). Used to get new ID/Access tokens when they expire (default 1 hour).

2. JWT Validation

JWTs are signed with RS256 (RSA + SHA-256). Validation steps:

  1. Decode the JWT header to get the kid (key ID)
  2. Fetch Cognito's public keys from: https://cognito-idp.{region}.amazonaws.com/{poolId}/.well-known/jwks.json
  3. Verify the signature using the matching public key
  4. Verify exp (not expired), iss (correct pool), aud (correct client)

3. Lambda Triggers

TriggerWhen it FiresCommon Use Case
Pre Sign-UpBefore creating the userValidate email domain, auto-confirm users
Post ConfirmationAfter user confirms emailCreate user profile in DynamoDB
Pre Token GenerationBefore issuing tokensAdd custom claims to JWT
Custom AuthenticationDefine custom auth challengeOTP, CAPTCHA, passwordless login
Post AuthenticationAfter successful sign-inAudit logging, update last-login

4. User Pool Groups & Roles

Assign users to Cognito Groups (e.g., Admins, Editors). Groups appear in the cognito:groups claim. Map groups to IAM roles in Identity Pool for AWS service access control.

5. OAuth 2.0 Flows

  • Authorization Code + PKCE: Recommended for SPAs and mobile apps. Most secure.
  • Implicit Flow: Deprecated. Avoid — tokens exposed in URL.
  • Client Credentials: Machine-to-machine (no user). For service accounts.

languages.label: Pre Token Trigger
languages.code:
import json
import boto3

dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb')
users_table = dynamodb.Table('Users')

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    """
    Pre Token Generation Lambda Trigger.
    Fires BEFORE Cognito issues tokens.
    Use it to add custom claims to the JWT.
    """
    trigger_source = event.get('triggerSource', '')
    user_sub       = event['request']['userAttributes'].get('sub')
    user_email     = event['request']['userAttributes'].get('email')

    # Add custom claims to the token
    # These appear in event.requestContext.authorizer.claims in Lambda
    event['response']['claimsOverrideDetails'] = {
        'claimsToAddOrOverride': {
            'custom:userId':   user_sub,
            'custom:email':    user_email,
            'custom:appRole':  _get_user_role(user_sub),
        },
        # Optionally suppress some default claims
        'claimsToSuppress': []
    }

    # CRITICAL: Must return the event object unchanged/modified
    return event

def _get_user_role(user_sub):
    """Fetch user role from DynamoDB and inject into JWT."""
    try:
        response = users_table.get_item(Key={'userId': user_sub})
        return response.get('Item', {}).get('role', 'viewer')
    except Exception:
        return 'viewer'


# =========================================================
# POST CONFIRMATION TRIGGER — runs after email verification
# =========================================================
def post_confirmation_handler(event, context):
    """
    Create a user profile in DynamoDB when a new user confirms their email.
    """
    attrs      = event['request']['userAttributes']
    user_sub   = attrs.get('sub')
    user_email = attrs.get('email')
    user_name  = attrs.get('name', user_email.split('@')[0])

    # Create profile in DynamoDB
    users_table.put_item(Item={
        'userId':    user_sub,
        'email':     user_email,
        'name':      user_name,
        'role':      'viewer',       # default role
        'createdAt': __import__('datetime').datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        'active':    True
    })

    # Return event unchanged — Cognito requires this
    return event

explanations.text: Pre Token Generation fires just before Cognito issues ID, Access, or Refresh tokens. The return value must be the event object with your modifications.
claimsOverrideDetails.claimsToAddOrOverride adds custom claims. These appear in the JWT payload and in event.requestContext.authorizer.claims in downstream Lambda.
CRITICAL: Every Cognito trigger must return the event object (possibly modified). Returning nothing or throwing causes the auth to fail.
Post Confirmation is the perfect place to initialize user resources. At this point the user email is verified and the user is committed to the system.

languages.label: JWT Validation
languages.code:
"""
Manual JWT validation in Lambda (no external libraries).
Used when you can't use API Gateway Cognito Authorizer
(e.g., WebSocket connections, custom auth flows).
"""
import json
import time
import base64
import hashlib
import urllib.request

# Cache the JWKS — fetched once per cold start
_JWKS_CACHE = {}
REGION    = __import__('os').environ.get('AWS_REGION', 'us-east-1')
POOL_ID   = __import__('os').environ.get('COGNITO_POOL_ID')
CLIENT_ID = __import__('os').environ.get('COGNITO_CLIENT_ID')

def validate_jwt(token):
    """
    Validates a Cognito JWT. Returns decoded claims or raises ValueError.
    """
    # 1. Split JWT into parts
    parts = token.split('.')
    if len(parts) != 3:
        raise ValueError("Invalid JWT format")

    # 2. Decode header to get key ID
    header = _decode_b64(parts[0])
    kid    = header.get('kid')
    alg    = header.get('alg', 'RS256')
    if alg != 'RS256':
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported algorithm: {alg}")

    # 3. Decode payload
    payload = _decode_b64(parts[1])

    # 4. Check expiration
    if payload.get('exp', 0) < time.time():
        raise ValueError("Token has expired")

    # 5. Check issuer matches our User Pool
    expected_iss = f"https://cognito-idp.{REGION}.amazonaws.com/{POOL_ID}"
    if payload.get('iss') != expected_iss:
        raise ValueError("Invalid token issuer")

    # 6. Check audience (client_id)
    if payload.get('aud') != CLIENT_ID and payload.get('client_id') != CLIENT_ID:
        raise ValueError("Invalid token audience")

    # NOTE: Signature verification requires a crypto library (cryptography/PyJWT)
    # In production, use: pip install python-jose[cryptography]
    # For API Gateway use cases, the Cognito Authorizer handles all of this natively.

    return payload

def _decode_b64(s):
    """Decode base64url-encoded JWT segment."""
    padding = 4 - len(s) % 4
    s = s + '=' * (padding % 4)
    return json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s))

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    auth_header = event.get('headers', {}).get('Authorization', '')
    if not auth_header.startswith('Bearer '):
        return {'statusCode': 401, 'body': json.dumps({'error': 'Missing Bearer token'})}

    token = auth_header[7:]
    try:
        claims = validate_jwt(token)
        user_id = claims.get('sub')
        return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps({'userId': user_id, 'claims': claims})}
    except ValueError as e:
        return {'statusCode': 401, 'body': json.dumps({'error': str(e)})}

questions.question: What is Amazon Cognito and what problem does it solve?
questions.shortAnswer: Amazon Cognito is a managed AWS service that handles user authentication, authorization, and user management with built-in sign-up/sign-in, MFA, and social login. It eliminates the need to build custom auth systems, manage passwords, handle MFA, and implement OAuth/OIDC.
questions.commonMistake: Not enabling MFA and strong password policies in production user pools.
questions.followUp: When would you NOT use Amazon Cognito?

questions.question: What are the key components of Amazon Cognito?
questions.shortAnswer: User Pools (authentication), Identity Pools (authorization), Lambda Triggers, Hosted UI, App Clients.
questions.commonMistake: Skipping IAM permissions configuration and using overly permissive policies.
questions.followUp: How does Amazon Cognito integrate with other AWS services?

questions.question: How is Amazon Cognito priced?
questions.shortAnswer: Priced based on usage — requests, data transfer, and provisioned capacity. Free tier available for 12 months.
questions.commonMistake: Not accounting for data transfer costs between services and regions.
questions.followUp: How do you estimate Amazon Cognito costs before deployment?

questions.question: What are the security best practices for Amazon Cognito?
questions.shortAnswer: Use least-privilege IAM policies, enable encryption at rest and in transit, use VPC endpoints where available, enable CloudTrail logging, and implement resource-based policies.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS managed policies that grant broader access than needed.
questions.followUp: How do you monitor Amazon Cognito for security events?

questions.question: How do you monitor Amazon Cognito?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudWatch metrics for operational monitoring, CloudWatch Logs for detailed logging, CloudTrail for API auditing, and set up alarms for critical thresholds.
questions.commonMistake: Not setting up alarms for error rates and latency — relying only on dashboards.
questions.followUp: What CloudWatch metrics are most important to monitor?

questions.question: How does Amazon Cognito achieve high availability?
questions.shortAnswer: Multi-AZ deployment, automatic failover, health checks, and data replication across Availability Zones.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying in single AZ for cost savings without understanding availability impact.
questions.followUp: What is the RPO and RTO for Amazon Cognito?

questions.question: Explain the Amazon Cognito scaling strategy.
questions.shortAnswer: Supports both vertical (instance size) and horizontal (instance count) scaling. Auto-scaling available based on CloudWatch metrics.
questions.commonMistake: Not load testing before production to determine correct scaling thresholds.
questions.followUp: How do you handle scaling during unexpected traffic spikes?

questions.question: How does Amazon Cognito handle encryption?
questions.shortAnswer: Supports encryption at rest (KMS keys) and in transit (TLS). Can use AWS-managed or customer-managed KMS keys. Key rotation supported.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS-managed keys when compliance requires customer-managed keys with custom key policies.
questions.followUp: How do you rotate encryption keys without downtime?

questions.question: What are the limits and quotas for Amazon Cognito?
questions.shortAnswer: Service has default quotas per region per account. Soft limits can be increased via Service Quotas. Hard limits cannot be changed.
questions.commonMistake: Hitting service limits during peak traffic without having requested increases in advance.
questions.followUp: How do you proactively monitor service quota usage?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon Cognito in a multi-account strategy?
questions.shortAnswer: Use AWS Organizations with SCPs, resource sharing via RAM where supported, cross-account IAM roles, and centralized logging.
questions.commonMistake: Not using separate accounts for production and development workloads.
questions.followUp: How do you share resources across accounts securely?

questions.question: Design a production-grade Amazon Cognito architecture.
questions.shortAnswer: Multi-AZ deployment, encryption, monitoring with alarms, automated backups, infrastructure as code (CloudFormation/Terraform), blue/green deployments, and disaster recovery plan.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying to production without a runbook for common failure scenarios.
questions.followUp: How do you test disaster recovery for this architecture?

questions.question: How do you optimize Amazon Cognito costs?
questions.shortAnswer: Right-size resources using CloudWatch metrics, use Reserved capacity for predictable workloads, implement auto-scaling, clean up unused resources, use Cost Explorer for analysis.
questions.commonMistake: Over-provisioning resources based on peak capacity estimates without actual usage data.
questions.followUp: How do you implement continuous cost optimization?

questions.question: What is the disaster recovery strategy for Amazon Cognito?
questions.shortAnswer: Pilot Light: core infrastructure in DR region. Warm Standby: scaled-down version running in DR region. Multi-Site: active-active across regions.
questions.commonMistake: Not regularly testing DR procedures — failover should be rehearsed quarterly.
questions.followUp: How do you automate DR failover?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon Cognito using Infrastructure as Code?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudFormation or Terraform to define resources declaratively. Include all dependencies (IAM roles, security groups, monitoring). Use parameters for environment-specific values.
questions.commonMistake: Not parameterizing templates — hardcoding account IDs, region, and environment-specific values.
questions.followUp: How do you handle state management in IaC for this service?

questions.question: What compliance frameworks does Amazon Cognito support?
questions.shortAnswer: SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FedRAMP. Use Config rules and Security Hub for continuous compliance monitoring.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming AWS compliance covers your application — shared responsibility model means you must secure your configuration.
questions.followUp: How do you generate compliance evidence for auditors?

questions.question: Your Amazon Cognito is experiencing intermittent errors. How do you diagnose?
questions.shortAnswer: Check CloudWatch metrics (error rate, latency, throttling), CloudWatch Logs for error details, X-Ray traces for request flow, CloudTrail for API changes, and service health dashboard.
questions.commonMistake: Only checking application logs without looking at AWS service-level metrics and limits.
questions.followUp: How do you set up proactive alerting for this service?

questions.question: Migrate Amazon Cognito from one AWS account to another.
questions.shortAnswer: Export configuration, create resources in target account via IaC, migrate data using service-specific tools, update DNS/endpoints, test, then cutover. Use cross-account roles during migration.
questions.commonMistake: Not planning for the DNS cutover — TTL should be lowered well before migration.
questions.followUp: How do you minimize downtime during migration?

questions.question: Amazon Cognito costs have doubled unexpectedly. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Cost Explorer → filter by service and usage type, check for unused resources, verify auto-scaling is working (not just scaling up), check for data transfer costs, review recent configuration changes.
questions.commonMistake: Only looking at compute costs and ignoring data transfer between services/regions.
questions.followUp: How do you set up billing alerts for this service?

questions.question: Design a zero-downtime update strategy for Amazon Cognito.
questions.shortAnswer: Blue/green deployment: create new version alongside old, test new version, switch traffic gradually (canary → full), rollback instantly if issues. Use CloudFormation update policies.
questions.commonMistake: Not having a rollback plan — every deployment should have a tested rollback procedure.
questions.followUp: How do you implement canary deployments?

questions.question: Your team needs to access Amazon Cognito across 5 AWS accounts. Design the access pattern.
questions.shortAnswer: IAM Identity Center with permission sets per account/role. Cross-account roles for programmatic access. Centralized logging account for audit. RAM for resource sharing where applicable.
questions.commonMistake: Creating separate IAM users in each account instead of using centralized SSO.
questions.followUp: How do you enforce least privilege across accounts?

questions.question: Amazon Cognito API calls are being throttled.
questions.shortAnswer: Implement exponential backoff with jitter, check service quotas and request increases, cache responses, use batch operations where available, distribute requests across time.
questions.commonMistake: Retrying throttled requests immediately without backoff, making the throttling worse.
questions.followUp: How do you design applications to be resilient to API throttling?

questions.question: Amazon Cognito has high latency. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: CloudWatch latency metrics, network connectivity (VPC endpoints vs internet), resource right-sizing, connection pooling, caching layer, regional endpoint proximity.
questions.commonMistake: Not using VPC endpoints — traffic going over internet instead of AWS backbone adds latency.
questions.followUp: How do you implement caching to reduce latency?

questions.question: Cannot access Amazon Cognito from Lambda function.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: Lambda execution role has required permissions, Lambda is in VPC with correct subnets/SG, VPC endpoint exists or NAT Gateway for internet access, resource-based policy allows Lambda.
questions.commonMistake: Putting Lambda in VPC without NAT Gateway or VPC endpoint — Lambda loses internet access.
questions.followUp: When should you put Lambda in a VPC vs outside VPC?

questions.question: Amazon Cognito encryption at rest is failing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: KMS key policy allows the service principal, key is in the same region, key is not disabled/pending deletion, IAM role has kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt permissions.
questions.commonMistake: Using a KMS key from a different region — KMS keys are regional.
questions.followUp: How do you troubleshoot KMS key policy issues?

questions.question: CloudWatch metrics for Amazon Cognito are missing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: detailed monitoring enabled (not just basic), correct namespace and metric name, data exists for the time range, metric dimensions correct, IAM permissions for CloudWatch.
questions.commonMistake: Looking at the wrong CloudWatch namespace or not enabling detailed monitoring.
questions.followUp: How do you create custom metrics for this service?

title: Amazon SQS — Message Queues
description: Message queuing, producer/consumer, visibility timeout, DLQ, and Lambda event source mapping.
subtitle: Amazon SQS — Reliable Message Queuing
objectives: Explain Standard vs FIFO queue differences and when to use each
Configure Lambda Event Source Mapping (ESM) to consume SQS messages
Understand visibility timeout and its relationship to Lambda timeout
Implement partial batch failure responses to handle errors correctly
Configure Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) to capture failed messages
Design producer and consumer Lambda functions
Monitor queue health with CloudWatch metrics (ApproximateNumberOfMessages, etc.)

content.html:
📨
Decouple, Buffer, and Protect
SQS decouples producers from consumers. If your downstream service is slow or offline, messages accumulate safely in the queue instead of being lost. It also protects Lambda from being overwhelmed by sudden traffic spikes.

The Core Problem SQS Solves

Without SQS: API Gateway → Lambda → Database. If the database is slow, Lambda waits. 10,000 concurrent requests hit Lambda simultaneously. Lambda concurrency limit hit → throttles. Requests lost.

With SQS: API → Lambda Producer → SQS Queue → Lambda Consumer (controlled concurrency) → Database. The queue absorbs spikes and consumer processes at a safe rate.

FeatureStandard QueueFIFO Queue
ThroughputUnlimited (nearly)300 TPS (3,000 with batching)
OrderingBest-effort (not guaranteed)Strict FIFO per Message Group
DeliveryAt-least-once (duplicates possible)Exactly-once processing
DeduplicationNot supported5-minute deduplication window
Use CaseEmail, notifications, logs, jobsFinancial transactions, order processing
⚠️
Standard Queue Idempotency Warning
Standard queues deliver messages AT LEAST ONCE. Your consumer Lambda must be idempotent — processing the same message twice should have the same effect as processing it once. Use DynamoDB conditional writes or check for existing records before processing.

content.title: SQS Event Source Mapping — Producer → Queue → Consumer

nodes.label: API / Event Source
nodes.description: Any event source: API Gateway, another Lambda, EventBridge, S3 events.

nodes.label: Producer Lambda
nodes.description: Sends messages to SQS using SendMessage or SendMessageBatch. Decoupled from consumer.

nodes.label: SQS Queue
nodes.description: Messages stored durably (up to 14 days). Lambda ESM polls the queue using long-polling. Visibility timeout hides messages during processing.

nodes.label: Dead-Letter Queue
nodes.description: Messages that fail maxReceiveCount times are moved to DLQ. Monitor DLQ depth as a critical alarm — non-zero DLQ means data loss is possible.

nodes.label: Consumer Lambda
nodes.description: Lambda ESM invokes the consumer with a batch of messages. Lambda has 6x concurrency scaling per minute from SQS.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.description: Consumer persists processed data.

content.html:
1. Event Source Mapping (ESM)

Lambda ESM is a service-side poller. Lambda's internal service polls SQS using long-polling (up to 20 seconds), retrieves messages in batches, and invokes your function. You don't write polling code.

2. Visibility Timeout

⏱️
Critical Setting: Visibility Timeout ≥ 6× Lambda Timeout
When Lambda receives a message, SQS hides it for the visibility timeout period. If Lambda doesn't complete before the timeout expires, SQS makes the message visible again — causing double-processing. Set visibility timeout to at least 6× your Lambda timeout.

3. Batch Processing & Partial Failure

Lambda receives a batch (2–10,000 messages). If Lambda throws any exception, ALL messages in the batch are retried — even successfully processed ones. Solutions:

  • ReportBatchItemFailures: Return {"batchItemFailures": [{"itemIdentifier": "msg-id"}]} to tell Lambda only specific messages failed.
  • Process individually: Catch exceptions per message and only add failures to the response.

4. Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ)

After maxReceiveCount failures, SQS moves the message to the DLQ. This prevents an infinite retry loop from blocking healthy messages. Key practices:

  • Always set a DLQ — otherwise messages are permanently lost after max retries
  • Set a CloudWatch alarm on DLQ depth > 0
  • Review DLQ messages regularly — they indicate bugs in your consumer

5. Long Polling

Lambda ESM uses long polling (WaitTimeSeconds=20) automatically. This reduces empty receives and costs. For SDK polling in your own code, always set WaitTimeSeconds=20.

6. Concurrency Scaling

Lambda ESM scales consumers up to 60 additional concurrent instances per minute, up to 1,000. Use reserved concurrency to limit consumer throughput and protect downstream services.

content.title: SQS Producer + Consumer with Partial Batch Failure

languages.label: Producer

explanations.text: QUEUE_URL from env var — never hardcode SQS URLs. The URL contains your account ID and region.
send_message for single messages. MessageGroupId is required for FIFO queues — groups ensure ordering within the same group.
send_message_batch sends up to 10 messages in one API call — 10× cheaper and faster than 10 individual sends.
Batch ID ('0', '1', ...) is required and must be unique within the batch. Different from the SQS MessageId.

languages.label: Consumer (Partial Failure)
languages.code:
import json
import boto3
import os
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb')
orders_table = dynamodb.Table(os.environ['ORDERS_TABLE'])

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    """
    Consumer Lambda — processes SQS messages with partial batch failure support.
    
    Returns batchItemFailures so only FAILED messages are retried,
    not the entire batch.
    """
    batch_item_failures = []

    for record in event['Records']:
        message_id = record['messageId']
        try:
            process_message(record)
            logger.info("Successfully processed: %s", message_id)

        except Exception as err:
            # Report ONLY this message as failed — others won't be retried
            logger.error("Failed to process %s: %s", message_id, str(err), exc_info=True)
            batch_item_failures.append({'itemIdentifier': message_id})

    # Return partial failure report
    # Empty list = all messages succeeded
    # Lambda deletes succeeded messages from queue automatically
    return {'batchItemFailures': batch_item_failures}


def process_message(record):
    """Process a single SQS record."""
    # Parse the message body
    body = json.loads(record['body'])
    order_id = body.get('orderId')
    user_id  = body.get('userId')
    amount   = body.get('amount', 0)

    if not order_id or not user_id:
        # Permanent failure — bad data. Don't retry (raise to move to DLQ after maxReceiveCount)
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid message: missing orderId or userId")

    # Idempotent write — use condition to avoid duplicate processing
    try:
        orders_table.put_item(
            Item={
                'PK': f'USER#{user_id}',
                'SK': f'ORDER#{order_id}',
                'orderId': order_id,
                'userId': user_id,
                'amount': amount,
                'status': 'RECEIVED',
                'sqsMessageId': record['messageId']
            },
            # Only write if item doesn't already exist — idempotency guard
            ConditionExpression='attribute_not_exists(PK)'
        )
    except dynamodb.meta.client.exceptions.ConditionalCheckFailedException:
        # Item already exists — message was already processed. This is OK.
        logger.warning("Duplicate message ignored: orderId=%s", order_id)

explanations.text: ESM invokes Lambda with event.Records containing a batch of SQS messages. Batch size is configured in the ESM settings (1–10,000).
Partial batch failure: catch per-message exceptions and add to batch_item_failures. Lambda will only retry failed messages, not the whole batch.
Return {"batchItemFailures": []} format — required for partial failure to work. ESM must be configured with FunctionResponseTypes: ["ReportBatchItemFailures"].
ConditionExpression attribute_not_exists(PK) makes the write idempotent — if the order already exists, DynamoDB raises ConditionalCheckFailedException instead of overwriting.

items.title: Messages processed multiple times
items.cause: Standard queue at-least-once delivery, or Lambda timeout exceeds visibility timeout causing re-delivery.
items.fix: Make consumer idempotent (ConditionExpression on DynamoDB). Set visibility timeout = 6× Lambda timeout. Use ReportBatchItemFailures.

items.title: Messages stuck in DLQ not processing
items.error: DLQ depth increasing, messages not being redriven
items.cause: DLQ messages are not automatically retried. Consumer bug is causing all messages to fail.
items.fix: Fix the consumer bug first. Use SQS Dead-Letter Queue Redrive (console or CLI) to replay DLQ messages back to source queue after fix.

items.title: Lambda scaling too fast — downstream overwhelmed
items.error: Database or downstream API getting too many requests
items.cause: Lambda ESM scales aggressively — 60 new instances per minute. If downstream has limited capacity, it gets overwhelmed.
items.fix: Set reserved concurrency on consumer Lambda to limit max concurrent executions. Use Batch Size and Maximum Batching Window to control throughput.

items.title: Messages not appearing in queue
items.error: send_message returns 200 but messages not visible
items.cause: Message may be in flight or delayed by Delivery Delay setting. Queue policy may restrict source.
items.fix: Check ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible. Set message delay to 0 for immediate delivery. Verify IAM/queue policy allows sqs:SendMessage from the source.

questions.question: Your Lambda consumer has a 5-minute (300s) timeout. What should you set the SQS visibility timeout to?

options.text: 300 seconds — match the Lambda timeout exactly
30 seconds — always use the SQS default
1800 seconds — set to 6× the Lambda timeout
Visibility timeout doesn't matter for Lambda ESM

questions.explanation: Visibility timeout must be at least 6× your Lambda timeout to prevent SQS from making the message visible again while Lambda is still processing it. For a 300s Lambda timeout: 300 × 6 = 1800 seconds. AWS recommends this exact formula.

questions.question: Lambda processes a batch of 10 SQS messages. Messages 3 and 7 fail to process. Without batchItemFailures configured, what happens?

options.text: Only messages 3 and 7 are retried; 1,2,4,5,6,8,9,10 are deleted
All 10 messages are retried because Lambda threw an exception
The entire batch is moved to the DLQ immediately
Messages are retried with exponential backoff

questions.explanation: Without ReportBatchItemFailures, if Lambda throws any exception, ALL messages in the batch return to the queue for retry — even the 8 that succeeded. This causes duplicate processing of successfully handled messages. Always implement batchItemFailures for SQS consumers.

questions.question: You need to process payment transactions in the exact order they were received. Which SQS queue type should you use?

options.text: Standard Queue with MessageDeduplicationId
FIFO Queue with MessageGroupId per user/account
Standard Queue with SQS delay queue
Standard Queue — ordering is guaranteed at high throughput

questions.explanation: FIFO queues guarantee strict ordering within a MessageGroup. For payments, use MessageGroupId = accountId so all transactions for the same account are processed in order. Standard queues provide best-effort ordering only and can deliver duplicates.

questions.question: What is Amazon SQS and what problem does it solve?
questions.shortAnswer: Amazon SQS is a managed AWS service that provides fully managed message queuing for decoupling and scaling distributed systems. It eliminates the need to manage message brokers like RabbitMQ, handle message persistence, and build retry logic.
questions.commonMistake: Not configuring Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) for messages that repeatedly fail processing.
questions.followUp: When would you NOT use Amazon SQS?

questions.question: What are the key components of Amazon SQS?
questions.shortAnswer: Standard Queue, FIFO Queue, Dead-Letter Queue, Message Groups, Visibility Timeout, Long Polling.
questions.commonMistake: Skipping IAM permissions configuration and using overly permissive policies.
questions.followUp: How does Amazon SQS integrate with other AWS services?

questions.question: How is Amazon SQS priced?
questions.shortAnswer: Priced based on usage — requests, data transfer, and provisioned capacity. Free tier available for 12 months.
questions.commonMistake: Not accounting for data transfer costs between services and regions.
questions.followUp: How do you estimate Amazon SQS costs before deployment?

questions.question: What are the security best practices for Amazon SQS?
questions.shortAnswer: Use least-privilege IAM policies, enable encryption at rest and in transit, use VPC endpoints where available, enable CloudTrail logging, and implement resource-based policies.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS managed policies that grant broader access than needed.
questions.followUp: How do you monitor Amazon SQS for security events?

questions.question: How do you monitor Amazon SQS?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudWatch metrics for operational monitoring, CloudWatch Logs for detailed logging, CloudTrail for API auditing, and set up alarms for critical thresholds.
questions.commonMistake: Not setting up alarms for error rates and latency — relying only on dashboards.
questions.followUp: What CloudWatch metrics are most important to monitor?

questions.question: How does Amazon SQS achieve high availability?
questions.shortAnswer: Messages stored redundantly across multiple AZs. 99.999999999% durability.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying in single AZ for cost savings without understanding availability impact.
questions.followUp: What is the RPO and RTO for Amazon SQS?

questions.question: Explain the Amazon SQS scaling strategy.
questions.shortAnswer: Supports both vertical (instance size) and horizontal (instance count) scaling. Auto-scaling available based on CloudWatch metrics.
questions.commonMistake: Not load testing before production to determine correct scaling thresholds.
questions.followUp: How do you handle scaling during unexpected traffic spikes?

questions.question: How does Amazon SQS handle encryption?
questions.shortAnswer: Supports encryption at rest (KMS keys) and in transit (TLS). Can use AWS-managed or customer-managed KMS keys. Key rotation supported.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS-managed keys when compliance requires customer-managed keys with custom key policies.
questions.followUp: How do you rotate encryption keys without downtime?

questions.question: What are the limits and quotas for Amazon SQS?
questions.shortAnswer: Service has default quotas per region per account. Soft limits can be increased via Service Quotas. Hard limits cannot be changed.
questions.commonMistake: Hitting service limits during peak traffic without having requested increases in advance.
questions.followUp: How do you proactively monitor service quota usage?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon SQS in a multi-account strategy?
questions.shortAnswer: Use AWS Organizations with SCPs, resource sharing via RAM where supported, cross-account IAM roles, and centralized logging.
questions.commonMistake: Not using separate accounts for production and development workloads.
questions.followUp: How do you share resources across accounts securely?

questions.question: Design a production-grade Amazon SQS architecture.
questions.shortAnswer: Multi-AZ deployment, encryption, monitoring with alarms, automated backups, infrastructure as code (CloudFormation/Terraform), blue/green deployments, and disaster recovery plan.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying to production without a runbook for common failure scenarios.
questions.followUp: How do you test disaster recovery for this architecture?

questions.question: How do you optimize Amazon SQS costs?
questions.shortAnswer: Right-size resources using CloudWatch metrics, use Reserved capacity for predictable workloads, implement auto-scaling, clean up unused resources, use Cost Explorer for analysis.
questions.commonMistake: Over-provisioning resources based on peak capacity estimates without actual usage data.
questions.followUp: How do you implement continuous cost optimization?

questions.question: What is the disaster recovery strategy for Amazon SQS?
questions.shortAnswer: Pilot Light: core infrastructure in DR region. Warm Standby: scaled-down version running in DR region. Multi-Site: active-active across regions.
questions.commonMistake: Not regularly testing DR procedures — failover should be rehearsed quarterly.
questions.followUp: How do you automate DR failover?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon SQS using Infrastructure as Code?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudFormation or Terraform to define resources declaratively. Include all dependencies (IAM roles, security groups, monitoring). Use parameters for environment-specific values.
questions.commonMistake: Not parameterizing templates — hardcoding account IDs, region, and environment-specific values.
questions.followUp: How do you handle state management in IaC for this service?

questions.question: What compliance frameworks does Amazon SQS support?
questions.shortAnswer: SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FedRAMP. Use Config rules and Security Hub for continuous compliance monitoring.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming AWS compliance covers your application — shared responsibility model means you must secure your configuration.
questions.followUp: How do you generate compliance evidence for auditors?

questions.question: Your Amazon SQS is experiencing intermittent errors. How do you diagnose?
questions.shortAnswer: Check CloudWatch metrics (error rate, latency, throttling), CloudWatch Logs for error details, X-Ray traces for request flow, CloudTrail for API changes, and service health dashboard.
questions.commonMistake: Only checking application logs without looking at AWS service-level metrics and limits.
questions.followUp: How do you set up proactive alerting for this service?

questions.question: Migrate Amazon SQS from one AWS account to another.
questions.shortAnswer: Export configuration, create resources in target account via IaC, migrate data using service-specific tools, update DNS/endpoints, test, then cutover. Use cross-account roles during migration.
questions.commonMistake: Not planning for the DNS cutover — TTL should be lowered well before migration.
questions.followUp: How do you minimize downtime during migration?

questions.question: Amazon SQS costs have doubled unexpectedly. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Cost Explorer → filter by service and usage type, check for unused resources, verify auto-scaling is working (not just scaling up), check for data transfer costs, review recent configuration changes.
questions.commonMistake: Only looking at compute costs and ignoring data transfer between services/regions.
questions.followUp: How do you set up billing alerts for this service?

questions.question: Design a zero-downtime update strategy for Amazon SQS.
questions.shortAnswer: Blue/green deployment: create new version alongside old, test new version, switch traffic gradually (canary → full), rollback instantly if issues. Use CloudFormation update policies.
questions.commonMistake: Not having a rollback plan — every deployment should have a tested rollback procedure.
questions.followUp: How do you implement canary deployments?

questions.question: Your team needs to access Amazon SQS across 5 AWS accounts. Design the access pattern.
questions.shortAnswer: IAM Identity Center with permission sets per account/role. Cross-account roles for programmatic access. Centralized logging account for audit. RAM for resource sharing where applicable.
questions.commonMistake: Creating separate IAM users in each account instead of using centralized SSO.
questions.followUp: How do you enforce least privilege across accounts?

questions.question: Amazon SQS API calls are being throttled.
questions.shortAnswer: Implement exponential backoff with jitter, check service quotas and request increases, cache responses, use batch operations where available, distribute requests across time.
questions.commonMistake: Retrying throttled requests immediately without backoff, making the throttling worse.
questions.followUp: How do you design applications to be resilient to API throttling?

questions.question: Amazon SQS has high latency. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: CloudWatch latency metrics, network connectivity (VPC endpoints vs internet), resource right-sizing, connection pooling, caching layer, regional endpoint proximity.
questions.commonMistake: Not using VPC endpoints — traffic going over internet instead of AWS backbone adds latency.
questions.followUp: How do you implement caching to reduce latency?

questions.question: Cannot access Amazon SQS from Lambda function.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: Lambda execution role has required permissions, Lambda is in VPC with correct subnets/SG, VPC endpoint exists or NAT Gateway for internet access, resource-based policy allows Lambda.
questions.commonMistake: Putting Lambda in VPC without NAT Gateway or VPC endpoint — Lambda loses internet access.
questions.followUp: When should you put Lambda in a VPC vs outside VPC?

questions.question: Amazon SQS encryption at rest is failing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: KMS key policy allows the service principal, key is in the same region, key is not disabled/pending deletion, IAM role has kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt permissions.
questions.commonMistake: Using a KMS key from a different region — KMS keys are regional.
questions.followUp: How do you troubleshoot KMS key policy issues?

questions.question: CloudWatch metrics for Amazon SQS are missing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: detailed monitoring enabled (not just basic), correct namespace and metric name, data exists for the time range, metric dimensions correct, IAM permissions for CloudWatch.
questions.commonMistake: Looking at the wrong CloudWatch namespace or not enabling detailed monitoring.
questions.followUp: How do you create custom metrics for this service?

title: Amazon SNS — Notifications & Fan-Out
description: Pub/sub messaging, fan-out patterns, message filtering, and Lambda subscriptions.
subtitle: Amazon SNS — Pub/Sub Messaging & Fan-Out
objectives: Explain SNS topics, subscriptions, and the publish/subscribe model
Implement Lambda functions as SNS subscribers
Design fan-out patterns using SNS → multiple SQS queues
Use message filtering to route messages to specific subscribers
Differentiate SNS from SQS and choose the right service
Handle SNS message format in Lambda (wrapped envelope)
Configure SNS dead-letter queues for failed deliveries

content.html:
📢
One Event → Many Consumers
SNS enables a single publish action to notify many subscribers simultaneously. Without SNS, you'd need to maintain a list of downstream services and call each one — tightly coupling your publisher to consumers.

SNS vs SQS — Which to Use?

AspectSNS (Pub/Sub)SQS (Queue)
PatternPush — SNS pushes to subscribersPull — consumer polls the queue
RecipientsMultiple subscribers simultaneouslyOne consumer per message
PersistenceNot persistent — deliver or fail (up to 3 retries)Persistent — up to 14 days
OrderingNo ordering guarantee (Standard) / FIFO topicFIFO queue guarantees order
Use CaseNotifications, fan-out, alertsAsync job processing, decoupling
💡
SNS + SQS = Best of Both Worlds
The most common pattern: SNS fan-out → multiple SQS queues. SNS delivers immediately to all queues (fan-out). SQS persists messages and Lambda processes them reliably. This combines SNS's broadcast with SQS's reliability.

nodes.label: Publisher Lambda
nodes.description: Any Lambda function (or service) publishes an event to the SNS topic with a single API call.

nodes.label: SNS Topic
nodes.description: SNS topic receives the message and fans it out to ALL subscribed endpoints simultaneously.

nodes.label: Email SQS Queue
nodes.description: Filtered subscription: receives only ORDER_PLACED events. Lambda consumer sends confirmation emails.

nodes.label: Inventory SQS
nodes.description: Filtered subscription: receives ORDER_PLACED and ORDER_CANCELLED events. Lambda updates inventory.

nodes.label: Analytics SQS
nodes.description: Unfiltered subscription: receives ALL events for data lake ingestion.

nodes.label: Email Lambda
nodes.description: Sends order confirmation email via SES.

nodes.label: Inventory Lambda
nodes.description: Decrements inventory in DynamoDB.

nodes.label: Analytics Lambda

content.html:
1. Topic & Subscription

A Topic is a communication channel. Subscriptions link the topic to endpoints (Lambda, SQS, HTTP, email, SMS, mobile push). When a message is published, SNS delivers it to ALL subscriptions concurrently.

2. Message Filtering

Subscription filter policies route messages based on message attributes — so each subscriber only receives relevant events. This avoids the need for consumers to check event type before processing.

// Email subscriber filter — only ORDER_PLACED events
{
  "eventType": ["ORDER_PLACED"]
}

// Inventory subscriber filter — ORDER_PLACED or ORDER_CANCELLED
{
  "eventType": ["ORDER_PLACED", "ORDER_CANCELLED"]
}

3. SNS Message Envelope in Lambda

When SNS directly invokes Lambda (without SQS), the Lambda event is an SNS envelope — the actual message is inside event.Records[0].Sns.Message as a JSON string.

4. SNS + SQS vs SNS → Lambda Direct

  • SNS → Lambda direct: No buffering. If Lambda is throttled or errors, SNS retries 3 times then discards.
  • SNS → SQS → Lambda: Messages are buffered in SQS. Lambda retries per SQS maxReceiveCount. DLQ available. Recommended for production.

5. Message Attributes vs Message Body

Filtering is based on message attributes (metadata), not the message body. Keep the body clean with your business payload. Put routing/type info in attributes.

6. SNS FIFO Topics

SNS FIFO topics maintain message ordering and deduplication within a message group. Must be used with SQS FIFO queues as subscribers. Use for ordered event streams like financial ledgers.

content.title: SNS Publisher + Lambda Subscriber Handler

languages.label: Publisher
languages.code:
import json
import boto3
import os
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

# Global SNS client
sns = boto3.client('sns')
ORDER_TOPIC_ARN = os.environ['ORDER_TOPIC_ARN']

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    """
    Publish order events to SNS topic.
    All downstream services (email, inventory, analytics) subscribe independently.
    """
    body = json.loads(event.get('body') or '{}')
    order_id  = body.get('orderId')
    event_type = body.get('eventType', 'ORDER_PLACED')
    amount    = body.get('amount', 0)

    if not order_id:
        return build_response(400, {'error': 'orderId required'})

    # Build the event payload
    message_payload = {
        'orderId':   order_id,
        'eventType': event_type,
        'amount':    amount,
        'timestamp': __import__('datetime').datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
    }

    # Publish to SNS — all subscribers receive this
    response = sns.publish(
        TopicArn=ORDER_TOPIC_ARN,
        Message=json.dumps(message_payload),
        Subject=f'Order Event: {event_type}',
        # MessageAttributes are used for subscription filtering
        MessageAttributes={
            'eventType': {
                'DataType': 'String',
                'StringValue': event_type
            },
            'orderAmount': {
                'DataType': 'Number',
                'StringValue': str(amount)
            }
        }
    )

    message_id = response['MessageId']
    logger.info("Published event: %s | MessageId: %s", event_type, message_id)

    return build_response(202, {
        'messageId': message_id,
        'event': event_type,
        'orderId': order_id
    })

def build_response(status, body):
    return {
        'statusCode': status,
        'headers': {'Content-Type': 'application/json'},
        'body': json.dumps(body)
    }

explanations.text: Publish the business payload as the Message body (JSON string). All subscribers get this.
Subject is optional — used for email subscriptions as the email subject line.
MessageAttributes are metadata used for subscription filter policies. Subscribers with a filter on eventType=ORDER_PLACED only receive matching messages.

languages.label: Subscriber (via SQS)
languages.code:
import json
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    """
    SNS → SQS → Lambda subscriber.
    
    When SNS delivers to SQS, the SQS message body is the SNS envelope.
    We must unwrap it to get our actual business payload.
    """
    for record in event['Records']:
        # SQS wraps the SNS message — unwrap it
        sqs_body = json.loads(record['body'])

        # SNS envelope fields
        sns_message_id = sqs_body.get('MessageId')
        topic_arn      = sqs_body.get('TopicArn')
        subject        = sqs_body.get('Subject', '')
        timestamp      = sqs_body.get('Timestamp')

        # The actual business payload is in 'Message' (another JSON string)
        payload = json.loads(sqs_body['Message'])
        order_id   = payload.get('orderId')
        event_type = payload.get('eventType')
        amount     = payload.get('amount', 0)

        logger.info(
            "Processing SNS event: type=%s orderId=%s msgId=%s",
            event_type, order_id, sns_message_id
        )

        # Route to appropriate handler based on event type
        if event_type == 'ORDER_PLACED':
            handle_order_placed(order_id, amount)
        elif event_type == 'ORDER_CANCELLED':
            handle_order_cancelled(order_id)
        else:
            logger.warning("Unknown event type: %s", event_type)

    return {'batchItemFailures': []}

def handle_order_placed(order_id, amount):
    logger.info("Updating inventory for order: %s (amount=$%.2f)", order_id, amount)
    # ... DynamoDB update inventory logic

def handle_order_cancelled(order_id):
    logger.info("Restoring inventory for cancelled order: %s", order_id)
    # ... DynamoDB restore inventory logic

explanations.text: SQS record body is the SNS envelope — a JSON object with SNS metadata plus the actual message in the "Message" field.
sqs_body["Message"] is our actual business payload as a JSON string. Double-decode: first SQS body, then SNS Message.
Route based on eventType — even though the subscription filter already narrowed this, defensive handling makes the function robust.

Updating inventory for order: ord-001 (amount=$59.99)

items.title: Lambda not receiving SNS messages
items.error: SNS publish succeeds but Lambda is never invoked
items.cause: Lambda resource-based policy does not allow sns.amazonaws.com to invoke it. Or subscription filter is too restrictive.
items.fix: Add resource-based policy: aws lambda add-permission --action lambda:InvokeFunction --principal sns.amazonaws.com. Verify filter policy matches your MessageAttributes.

items.title: Messages lost after SNS publish
items.error: Messages published but no delivery confirmation
items.cause: SNS → Lambda direct: Lambda was throttled, SNS retried 3 times and discarded. No DLQ configured.
items.fix: Use SNS → SQS → Lambda instead. SQS persists messages through Lambda throttling and retries. Configure subscription DLQ (redrive policy on SQS or SNS subscription DLQ).

items.title: SNS message body not parsing correctly
items.cause: Common mistake: trying to json.loads the SQS body directly without unwrapping the SNS envelope first.
items.fix: Double-decode: first sqs_body = json.loads(record["body"]), then payload = json.loads(sqs_body["Message"]). The SNS envelope wraps your payload in the "Message" field.

items.title: Filter policy not working
items.error: All subscribers receive all messages despite filter
items.cause: Filter policy is on message body fields, not MessageAttributes. SNS filtering only works on MessageAttributes.
items.fix: Move filter criteria to MessageAttributes when publishing: MessageAttributes={"eventType": {"DataType": "String", "StringValue": "ORDER_PLACED"}}

questions.question: You publish an order event to SNS. You have 3 SQS subscribers with different filter policies. What happens if the message matches filters for subscribers 1 and 2 but NOT subscriber 3?

options.text: All 3 queues receive the message
Only subscriber 1 and 2 queues receive the message; subscriber 3 does not
No messages are delivered — all filters must match
SNS throws an error if any filter fails

questions.explanation: SNS filter policies are per-subscription. SNS evaluates each subscription's filter independently and delivers only to matching subscriptions. Subscribers with non-matching filters simply don't receive the message — this is the whole point of filtering.

questions.question: Your Lambda SNS subscriber throws an exception. SNS retries delivery. What happens after all retries are exhausted with no DLQ configured?

options.text: The message is stored for 24 hours and retried later
The message is permanently lost
SNS falls back to email delivery
The message is sent back to the publisher

questions.explanation: SNS direct Lambda delivery: SNS retries 3 times with exponential backoff. After all retries, if no DLQ is configured on the subscription, the message is permanently discarded. This is why SNS → SQS → Lambda is preferred in production — SQS adds persistence.

questions.question: When Lambda processes an SQS message that came from SNS (SNS → SQS → Lambda), where is your actual business data in the event?

options.text: event.Records[0].body directly
event.Records[0].Sns.Message
json.loads(event.Records[0].body)["Message"]
event.Records[0].attributes.Message

questions.explanation: SNS → SQS → Lambda involves double-wrapping: SQS record body contains the SNS envelope JSON. Inside that is the "Message" field (string) containing your actual payload. You must parse twice: body = json.loads(record["body"]), then payload = json.loads(body["Message"]).

questions.question: What is Amazon SNS and what problem does it solve?
questions.shortAnswer: Amazon SNS is a managed AWS service that provides pub/sub messaging for sending notifications to multiple subscribers (Lambda, SQS, HTTP, email, SMS). It eliminates the need to build custom notification systems, manage fan-out logic, and handle subscriber management.
questions.commonMistake: Not using message filtering — all subscribers receive all messages without it.
questions.followUp: When would you NOT use Amazon SNS?

questions.question: What are the key components of Amazon SNS?
questions.shortAnswer: Topics, Subscriptions, Message Filtering, Dead-Letter Queue, FIFO Topics, Message Attributes.
questions.commonMistake: Skipping IAM permissions configuration and using overly permissive policies.
questions.followUp: How does Amazon SNS integrate with other AWS services?

questions.question: How is Amazon SNS priced?
questions.shortAnswer: Priced based on usage — requests, data transfer, and provisioned capacity. Free tier available for 12 months.
questions.commonMistake: Not accounting for data transfer costs between services and regions.
questions.followUp: How do you estimate Amazon SNS costs before deployment?

questions.question: What are the security best practices for Amazon SNS?
questions.shortAnswer: Use least-privilege IAM policies, enable encryption at rest and in transit, use VPC endpoints where available, enable CloudTrail logging, and implement resource-based policies.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS managed policies that grant broader access than needed.
questions.followUp: How do you monitor Amazon SNS for security events?

questions.question: How do you monitor Amazon SNS?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudWatch metrics for operational monitoring, CloudWatch Logs for detailed logging, CloudTrail for API auditing, and set up alarms for critical thresholds.
questions.commonMistake: Not setting up alarms for error rates and latency — relying only on dashboards.
questions.followUp: What CloudWatch metrics are most important to monitor?

questions.question: How does Amazon SNS achieve high availability?
questions.shortAnswer: Multi-AZ deployment, automatic failover, health checks, and data replication across Availability Zones.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying in single AZ for cost savings without understanding availability impact.
questions.followUp: What is the RPO and RTO for Amazon SNS?

questions.question: Explain the Amazon SNS scaling strategy.
questions.shortAnswer: Supports both vertical (instance size) and horizontal (instance count) scaling. Auto-scaling available based on CloudWatch metrics.
questions.commonMistake: Not load testing before production to determine correct scaling thresholds.
questions.followUp: How do you handle scaling during unexpected traffic spikes?

questions.question: How does Amazon SNS handle encryption?
questions.shortAnswer: Supports encryption at rest (KMS keys) and in transit (TLS). Can use AWS-managed or customer-managed KMS keys. Key rotation supported.
questions.commonMistake: Using AWS-managed keys when compliance requires customer-managed keys with custom key policies.
questions.followUp: How do you rotate encryption keys without downtime?

questions.question: What are the limits and quotas for Amazon SNS?
questions.shortAnswer: Service has default quotas per region per account. Soft limits can be increased via Service Quotas. Hard limits cannot be changed.
questions.commonMistake: Hitting service limits during peak traffic without having requested increases in advance.
questions.followUp: How do you proactively monitor service quota usage?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon SNS in a multi-account strategy?
questions.shortAnswer: Use AWS Organizations with SCPs, resource sharing via RAM where supported, cross-account IAM roles, and centralized logging.
questions.commonMistake: Not using separate accounts for production and development workloads.
questions.followUp: How do you share resources across accounts securely?

questions.question: Design a production-grade Amazon SNS architecture.
questions.shortAnswer: Multi-AZ deployment, encryption, monitoring with alarms, automated backups, infrastructure as code (CloudFormation/Terraform), blue/green deployments, and disaster recovery plan.
questions.commonMistake: Deploying to production without a runbook for common failure scenarios.
questions.followUp: How do you test disaster recovery for this architecture?

questions.question: How do you optimize Amazon SNS costs?
questions.shortAnswer: Right-size resources using CloudWatch metrics, use Reserved capacity for predictable workloads, implement auto-scaling, clean up unused resources, use Cost Explorer for analysis.
questions.commonMistake: Over-provisioning resources based on peak capacity estimates without actual usage data.
questions.followUp: How do you implement continuous cost optimization?

questions.question: What is the disaster recovery strategy for Amazon SNS?
questions.shortAnswer: Pilot Light: core infrastructure in DR region. Warm Standby: scaled-down version running in DR region. Multi-Site: active-active across regions.
questions.commonMistake: Not regularly testing DR procedures — failover should be rehearsed quarterly.
questions.followUp: How do you automate DR failover?

questions.question: How do you implement Amazon SNS using Infrastructure as Code?
questions.shortAnswer: Use CloudFormation or Terraform to define resources declaratively. Include all dependencies (IAM roles, security groups, monitoring). Use parameters for environment-specific values.
questions.commonMistake: Not parameterizing templates — hardcoding account IDs, region, and environment-specific values.
questions.followUp: How do you handle state management in IaC for this service?

questions.question: What compliance frameworks does Amazon SNS support?
questions.shortAnswer: SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FedRAMP. Use Config rules and Security Hub for continuous compliance monitoring.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming AWS compliance covers your application — shared responsibility model means you must secure your configuration.
questions.followUp: How do you generate compliance evidence for auditors?

questions.question: Your Amazon SNS is experiencing intermittent errors. How do you diagnose?
questions.shortAnswer: Check CloudWatch metrics (error rate, latency, throttling), CloudWatch Logs for error details, X-Ray traces for request flow, CloudTrail for API changes, and service health dashboard.
questions.commonMistake: Only checking application logs without looking at AWS service-level metrics and limits.
questions.followUp: How do you set up proactive alerting for this service?

questions.question: Migrate Amazon SNS from one AWS account to another.
questions.shortAnswer: Export configuration, create resources in target account via IaC, migrate data using service-specific tools, update DNS/endpoints, test, then cutover. Use cross-account roles during migration.
questions.commonMistake: Not planning for the DNS cutover — TTL should be lowered well before migration.
questions.followUp: How do you minimize downtime during migration?

questions.question: Amazon SNS costs have doubled unexpectedly. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Cost Explorer → filter by service and usage type, check for unused resources, verify auto-scaling is working (not just scaling up), check for data transfer costs, review recent configuration changes.
questions.commonMistake: Only looking at compute costs and ignoring data transfer between services/regions.
questions.followUp: How do you set up billing alerts for this service?

questions.question: Design a zero-downtime update strategy for Amazon SNS.
questions.shortAnswer: Blue/green deployment: create new version alongside old, test new version, switch traffic gradually (canary → full), rollback instantly if issues. Use CloudFormation update policies.
questions.commonMistake: Not having a rollback plan — every deployment should have a tested rollback procedure.
questions.followUp: How do you implement canary deployments?

questions.question: Your team needs to access Amazon SNS across 5 AWS accounts. Design the access pattern.
questions.shortAnswer: IAM Identity Center with permission sets per account/role. Cross-account roles for programmatic access. Centralized logging account for audit. RAM for resource sharing where applicable.
questions.commonMistake: Creating separate IAM users in each account instead of using centralized SSO.
questions.followUp: How do you enforce least privilege across accounts?

questions.question: Amazon SNS API calls are being throttled.
questions.shortAnswer: Implement exponential backoff with jitter, check service quotas and request increases, cache responses, use batch operations where available, distribute requests across time.
questions.commonMistake: Retrying throttled requests immediately without backoff, making the throttling worse.
questions.followUp: How do you design applications to be resilient to API throttling?

questions.question: Amazon SNS has high latency. Investigate.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: CloudWatch latency metrics, network connectivity (VPC endpoints vs internet), resource right-sizing, connection pooling, caching layer, regional endpoint proximity.
questions.commonMistake: Not using VPC endpoints — traffic going over internet instead of AWS backbone adds latency.
questions.followUp: How do you implement caching to reduce latency?

questions.question: Cannot access Amazon SNS from Lambda function.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: Lambda execution role has required permissions, Lambda is in VPC with correct subnets/SG, VPC endpoint exists or NAT Gateway for internet access, resource-based policy allows Lambda.
questions.commonMistake: Putting Lambda in VPC without NAT Gateway or VPC endpoint — Lambda loses internet access.
questions.followUp: When should you put Lambda in a VPC vs outside VPC?

questions.question: Amazon SNS encryption at rest is failing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: KMS key policy allows the service principal, key is in the same region, key is not disabled/pending deletion, IAM role has kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt permissions.
questions.commonMistake: Using a KMS key from a different region — KMS keys are regional.
questions.followUp: How do you troubleshoot KMS key policy issues?

questions.question: CloudWatch metrics for Amazon SNS are missing.
questions.shortAnswer: Check: detailed monitoring enabled (not just basic), correct namespace and metric name, data exists for the time range, metric dimensions correct, IAM permissions for CloudWatch.
questions.commonMistake: Looking at the wrong CloudWatch namespace or not enabling detailed monitoring.
questions.followUp: How do you create custom metrics for this service?

title: Amazon EventBridge — Event-Driven Architecture
description: Event-driven architecture, event buses, rules, patterns, scheduler, and Lambda targets.
subtitle: Amazon EventBridge — Event-Driven Architecture
objectives: Explain EventBridge event buses (default, custom, partner) and when to use each
Write event pattern rules to filter and route events to Lambda targets
Publish custom events to EventBridge from Lambda
Use EventBridge Scheduler to replace CloudWatch Events cron jobs
Implement content-based routing with complex filter patterns
Design event-driven microservices with EventBridge as the backbone
Monitor EventBridge with CloudWatch metrics and archive events for replay

content.html:
🔔
The Event Router for AWS
EventBridge is a serverless event bus that routes events from AWS services, your applications, and SaaS providers to targets. Unlike SNS (point-to-point fan-out), EventBridge enables complex content-based routing, transformation, and replay without any code changes to publishers.
FeatureSNSEventBridge
RoutingTopic + subscription filtersContent-based rules on any event field
Event SourcesYour code (explicit publish)200+ AWS services emit automatically
Schema Registry❌✅ Auto-discovers and stores event schemas
Event Archive❌✅ Archive for replay (debugging, migration)
Input Transformation❌✅ Transform event before delivery to target
Dead Letter QueueSubscription-level DLQRule target DLQ
Partner Events❌✅ Datadog, GitHub, Shopify, Stripe, etc.
Scheduler❌✅ One-time and recurring schedules
💡
EventBridge is the Modern CloudWatch Events
CloudWatch Events is now EventBridge. The default event bus IS CloudWatch Events. All your CloudWatch Events rules appear in EventBridge. EventBridge adds custom buses, schema registry, pipes, and Scheduler on top.

nodes.label: AWS Services
nodes.description: AWS services automatically emit events to the default event bus: EC2 state changes, S3 events, CodePipeline stage changes, ECS task state changes, etc.

nodes.label: Custom App Lambda
nodes.description: Your Lambda functions publish custom events to a custom event bus using PutEvents API.

nodes.label: EventBridge Bus
nodes.description: Event bus receives events from all sources. Rules evaluate each incoming event against their patterns and route matching events to configured targets.

nodes.label: Rule: Premium Orders
nodes.description: Pattern: {"source": ["com.myapp.orders"], "detail": {"tier": ["premium"]}}. Only premium orders trigger this rule.

nodes.label: Rule: All Orders
nodes.description: Pattern: {"source": ["com.myapp.orders"]}. Matches all order events regardless of tier.

nodes.label: Scheduled Rule
nodes.description: Cron expression: cron(0 9 * * ? *). Fires every day at 9am UTC to trigger daily reports.

nodes.label: VIP Lambda
nodes.description: Sends VIP treatment email for premium orders.

nodes.label: Analytics Lambda
nodes.description: Records all orders to data warehouse.

nodes.label: Report Lambda
nodes.description: Generates and sends daily summary report.

content.html:
1. Event Buses

  • Default Bus: AWS service events. One per region per account. Cannot be deleted.
  • Custom Bus: Your application events. Create separate buses per domain (orders, users, payments) for clear ownership.
  • Partner Bus: SaaS partner events (Datadog, Shopify, GitHub). No publish code needed — partners push directly.

2. Event Structure

Every EventBridge event has the same envelope:

{
  "version": "0",
  "id": "12345678-1234-1234-1234-123456789012",
  "source": "com.myapp.orders",      // Who sent it
  "account": "123456789012",
  "time": "2026-09-16T02:00:00Z",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "detail-type": "OrderPlaced",     // What happened
  "detail": {                        // Your business payload
    "orderId": "ord-001",
    "amount": 99.99,
    "tier": "premium"
  }
}

3. Event Patterns (Rules)

Rules filter events using pattern matching. Patterns can match on any field including nested detail fields:

// Simple pattern — all order events
{"source": ["com.myapp.orders"]}

// Content-based — premium orders only
{"source": ["com.myapp.orders"], "detail": {"tier": ["premium"]}}

// Numeric range — orders over $100
{"detail": {"amount": [{"numeric": [">", 100]}]}}

// Prefix match — any EC2 event
{"source": ["aws.ec2"]}

4. Input Transformation

Transform the event before delivering to the target — reshape the payload without Lambda code:

// Input transformer — extract only what Lambda needs
InputPathsMap: {"orderId": "$.detail.orderId", "amount": "$.detail.amount"}
InputTemplate: '{"order": "", "value": ""}'

5. EventBridge Scheduler

Replaces cron-based CloudWatch Events for invoking Lambda on a schedule. Supports:

  • Cron expressions: cron(0 9 * * ? *) — 9am UTC daily
  • Rate expressions: rate(5 minutes)
  • One-time schedules: Specific date/time (great for deferred jobs)

6. Archive & Replay

Archive events for any period (or indefinitely). Replay archived events to a bus to:

  • Debug production issues by re-processing historical events
  • Backfill new services when they come online
  • Test new rule configurations against real historical data

languages.label: Publisher
languages.code:
import json
import boto3
import os
import logging
from datetime import datetime

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

# Global EventBridge client
events = boto3.client('events')
EVENT_BUS_NAME = os.environ.get('EVENT_BUS_NAME', 'default')

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    """
    Publish custom events to EventBridge.
    Called after order is created in DynamoDB.
    """
    body = json.loads(event.get('body') or '{}')
    order_id = body.get('orderId')
    user_id  = body.get('userId')
    amount   = body.get('amount', 0)
    tier     = 'premium' if amount >= 100 else 'standard'

    # Build EventBridge event entries
    entries = [
        {
            'Source': 'com.myapp.orders',
            'DetailType': 'OrderPlaced',
            'Detail': json.dumps({
                'orderId':   order_id,
                'userId':    user_id,
                'amount':    amount,
                'tier':      tier,
                'timestamp': datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
            }),
            'EventBusName': EVENT_BUS_NAME,
            # Optional: resources this event relates to
            'Resources': [
                f'arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:123456789012:table/Orders/item/{order_id}'
            ]
        }
    ]

    # PutEvents supports up to 10 entries per call
    response = events.put_events(Entries=entries)

    failed = response.get('FailedEntryCount', 0)
    if failed > 0:
        logger.error("EventBridge failures: %s", response['Entries'])
        return build_response(500, {'error': 'Failed to publish events'})

    entry = response['Entries'][0]
    event_id = entry.get('EventId')
    logger.info("Published OrderPlaced: eventId=%s orderId=%s tier=%s",
                event_id, order_id, tier)

    return build_response(202, {
        'eventId': event_id,
        'orderId': order_id,
        'tier': tier
    })

def build_response(status, body):
    return {
        'statusCode': status,
        'headers': {'Content-Type': 'application/json'},
        'body': json.dumps(body)
    }

explanations.text: "Source" is your application identifier. Use reverse-domain notation (com.company.domain) to avoid conflicts with AWS sources (aws.*).
"DetailType" describes WHAT happened in human-readable terms. Think of it as the event name. Consumers use this for routing and logging.
"Detail" is your business payload as a JSON string. EventBridge limits Detail to 256 KB.
PutEvents accepts up to 10 events per call. FailedEntryCount > 0 means some events failed — inspect Entries[i].ErrorCode and ErrorMessage.

explanations.text: CRITICAL DIFFERENCE: EventBridge invokes Lambda with the full event envelope directly — no Records wrapper, no Sns envelope. event IS the EventBridge event object.
"detail-type" (with hyphen) not "detail_type". Python dicts use the key as-is from JSON. Must use event.get("detail-type").
"detail" is already a Python dict (EventBridge parses it from JSON string before delivery). No json.loads() needed.
EventBridge invokes Lambda asynchronously. Return value is ignored. Lambda must handle idempotency — EventBridge may retry on throttle or error.

content.initialText:
EventBridge CLI Lab. Try:

items.title: Events published but Lambda not invoked
items.cause: Rule pattern doesn't match the event. Most common: source or detail-type has a typo, or detail fields don't match the pattern structure.
items.fix: Use EventBridge console "Test event pattern" tool with a sample event. Check that source, detail-type, and detail field values exactly match. Remember: patterns use arrays for values (["ORDER_PLACED"] not "ORDER_PLACED").

items.title: Lambda lacks permission to be invoked by EventBridge
items.cause: Lambda resource-based policy doesn't allow events.amazonaws.com to invoke the function.
items.fix: Add resource policy: aws lambda add-permission --action lambda:InvokeFunction --principal events.amazonaws.com --source-arn arn:aws:events:...:rule/your-rule-name

items.title: FailedEntryCount > 0 in PutEvents
items.cause: Individual entries in the batch failed: missing required fields (Source, DetailType, Detail), Detail > 256KB, or invalid bus name.
items.fix: Check Entries[i].ErrorCode and ErrorMessage for each failed entry. Each entry fails/succeeds independently. Re-send only the failed entries.

items.title: Scheduled rule not firing at expected time
items.cause: EventBridge cron uses UTC timezone (? for day-of-week or day-of-month), not the local timezone. Common mistake: cron(0 9 * * ? *) fires at 9am UTC, not local time.
items.fix: Convert your local time to UTC. Use EventBridge Scheduler for timezone-aware scheduling with named timezones (e.g., America/New_York).

questions.question: You publish events with source="com.myapp.orders" and detail.tier="premium". Your EventBridge rule pattern is {"source": ["com.myapp.orders"], "detail": {"tier": ["premium"]}}. Will this rule match?

options.text: No — detail must use prefix matching, not exact match
Yes — the source and detail.tier both match the pattern arrays
No — you cannot filter on nested detail fields
Yes, but only if the event is on the default bus

questions.explanation: EventBridge patterns match when ALL specified fields match. Array values in patterns mean "any of these values". source matches "com.myapp.orders" ✓, detail.tier matches "premium" ✓. Both match → rule fires.

questions.question: How does Lambda receive an EventBridge event delivered via a rule, compared to an SQS message?

options.text: EventBridge uses event.Records[0].detail, SQS uses event.Records[0].body
EventBridge delivers the full event envelope directly as the Lambda event (no Records wrapper). SQS uses event.Records[].
They use the same format — both have event.Records[]
EventBridge only invokes Lambda via SQS queue, not directly

questions.explanation: Critical difference: EventBridge delivers the event directly — event.source, event["detail-type"], event.detail are top-level fields. SQS uses event.Records[]. SNS (direct) also uses event.Records[]. Always check the specific trigger type in the Lambda docs.

questions.question: You want to trigger a Lambda at 6pm New York time every weekday. What is the best approach?

options.text: Use EventBridge rule with cron(0 18 ? * MON-FRI *) — EventBridge handles timezone conversion
Calculate UTC offset and use EventBridge Scheduler with America/New_York timezone
Use a Lambda running every minute that checks the current time
EventBridge schedules cannot target specific timezones

questions.explanation: EventBridge Scheduler (not Rules) supports named timezones like America/New_York. Rules cron expressions only support UTC. For timezone-aware scheduling, always use EventBridge Scheduler, which handles DST transitions automatically.
